shape.subject: Mathematics
shape.scope: Numbers and their operations (primes, HCF/LCM, squares/cubes/roots, standard form, estimation, significant figures); ratio and proportion (incl. map scales, direct and inverse proportion); percentage (incl. reverse percentage); rate and speed (incl. average speed, conversion of units); financial mathematics (simple and compound interest, hire purchase, money exchange, taxation, utilities bills); algebraic expressions and formulae (expansion, factorisation incl. grouping and quadratic trinomials, algebraic fractions, changing the subject, algebraic identities); functions and graphs (linear, quadratic incl. completed-square and factorised forms, cubic, reciprocal y=a/x and a/x^2, exponential y=ka^x, drawing on a grid from a table of values, gradient of a curve by a tangent, solving equations by drawing a suitable line); equations and inequalities (linear, simultaneous linear, quadratic by factorisation / completing the square / the formula, fractional equations reducing to quadratics, linear inequalities incl. double inequalities, word problems leading to these); set language and notation (union, intersection, complement, subsets, Venn diagrams with numbers of elements); matrices (display of information, addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication of two matrices, interpretation of the product; no inverses); problems in real-world contexts (reading tables and information sheets, making and justifying a decision, estimating a cost or a quantity); angles, triangles and polygons (angle properties of parallel lines, triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons; construction with ruler, compasses and protractor: perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors; scale drawings); congruence and similarity (tests, ratios of lengths, areas and volumes of similar figures and solids); properties of circles (symmetry properties: equal chords, perpendicular from centre, tangents from a point; angle properties: angle at centre, angle in a semicircle, angles in the same segment, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, tangent-radius; reasons stated); Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry (sine, cosine and tangent for acute and obtuse angles, sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle as ½ab sin C, bearings, angles of elevation and depression, simple 3-D problems); mensuration (area of a triangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle; arc length and sector area with the angle in RADIANS or degrees; surface area and volume of a prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone and sphere; composite solids); coordinate geometry (gradient, length, midpoint is NOT required, equation of a straight line y=mx+c, parallel lines, area of a rectilinear figure by shoelace is NOT required — use base×height or split into triangles); vectors in two dimensions (column vectors, magnitude, position vectors, addition, scalar multiples, collinearity, expressing one vector in terms of others, ratios of areas of triangles with a common height or on the same base); data handling and analysis (tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, line graphs, histograms with equal class widths, dot diagrams, stem-and-leaf, box-and-whisker plots, cumulative frequency curves, median, quartiles, percentiles, range, interquartile range, mean and standard deviation for grouped and ungrouped data, comparing two distributions in context); probability (single events, combined events by possibility diagrams and tree diagrams, with and without replacement, mutually exclusive and independent events). NOT in 4052: calculus, logarithms, surds, the binomial theorem, trigonometric identities, the R-formula, quadratic inequalities, matrices inverses and determinants, vectors in three dimensions, the shoelace formula, the midpoint formula.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks (4052)
- Plain, exact, economical English. Instructions are imperatives: Find, Calculate, Work out, Write down, Simplify, Factorise, Expand, Solve, Show that, Explain why, Give a reason, Complete the table, Draw, Describe, Estimate, Express, State.
- Parts are labelled (a), (b), (c), with sub-parts (i), (ii). Every part carries its marks. A 1–3 mark question is often a single unlabelled part.
- A scientific calculator is allowed on BOTH papers. Never write "a calculator must not be used". The paper's rubric already says: non-exact answers to 3 significant figures, angles to 1 decimal place, π = calculator value or 3.142 — so a question states a precision only when it wants something else ("correct to 2 decimal places", "in its simplest form", "in terms of π", "as a fraction in its lowest terms", "in standard form", "to the nearest cent").
- Angles are in DEGREES with the degree sign ($58^\circ$); a sector angle in radians is stated as "1.8 radians". Bearings are three-figure ($048^\circ$). Money is dollars and cents ($\$92.75$).
- Contexts are short, concrete and Singaporean-neutral (a garden fountain, a box of apples, a map of Singapore, a candle business): the situation in one or two sentences, units given, then the parts. Never chatty, never a story.
- "Show that" states its target exactly ("Show that $x^2 - 102x + 1440 = 0$", "Show that $p = 2.5$") and a later part uses it. "Explain why …" / "Give a reason for your answer" / "Is he correct?" parts are worth 1 mark and expect one sentence with a number in it. A circle-properties question says "Give a reason for each step of your working."
- Statistics and probability parts ask for interpretation in context ("By commenting on the means and the standard deviations, compare …", "Explain what this tells you about …").
- Paper 1 (27 short questions, 90 marks): each question tests ONE idea in 1–7 marks, answered in the space provided; the paper walks the syllabus (number, algebra, geometry, statistics interleaved), with the vector and mensuration questions near the end.
- Paper 2 (9 long questions, 90 marks): each question is 8–12 marks in 3–5 parts. Early questions are ALGEBRA MEDLEYS whose parts (a), (b), (c), (d) are separate short problems on different algebra skills. Later ones are one context developed through parts: a graph question (a table of values with two blanks, "On the grid, draw the graph of …", a gradient by a tangent, "By drawing a suitable straight line, solve …"), a trigonometry-on-the-ground question with bearings and a mast, a statistics + probability question over a table or histogram, a circle-properties + circular-measure question, a speed/quadratic question ("Show that … = 0", solve to 2 decimal places, reject a root, interpret), and the last question is a PROBLEM IN A REAL-WORLD CONTEXT: an information sheet (a table of prices, rates or measurements) followed by parts that end in a 5–7 mark "Suggest a suitable … Justify your answer" or "Is it worth …? Show your working" decision.
- Marks follow the work: about 1 mark per 1.5 minutes. 1 mark: read/state/one-line. 2 marks: one routine. 3–4 marks: a short chain. 5–7 marks: a multi-step argument or a decision with working.

title: E Math · Set 2 · Paper 1 · O-Level format

question.stem:
When $\dfrac{x + 6}{3}$ is subtracted from $\dfrac{3x - 2}{4}$, the result is 5.
Find the value of $x$.
skills: translate 'A is subtracted from B' into B minus A, the order reversed from the wording
clear two numerical denominators with the unknown in both numerators, expanding a bracket preceded by a minus sign
question.solution:
$\dfrac{3x - 2}{4} - \dfrac{x + 6}{3} = 5$
Multiply both sides by 12:
$3(3x - 2) - 4(x + 6) = 60$  (M1: this equation, or an equivalent equation in the correct order with the denominators cleared)
$9x - 6 - 4x - 24 = 60$
$5x - 30 = 60$
$5x = 90$
$x = 18$  (A1: $x = 18$)
Check: $\dfrac{3(18) - 2}{4} = 13$ and $\dfrac{18 + 6}{3} = 8$, and $13 - 8 = 5$.
Common errors: subtracting in the wrong order, $\dfrac{x + 6}{3} - \dfrac{3x - 2}{4} = 5$, gives $4x + 24 - 9x + 6 = 60$, so $x = -6$ (tidy but wrong); writing $-4(x + 6)$ as $-4x + 24$ gives $5x = 42$.
Mark scheme: M1 for $3(3x - 2) - 4(x + 6) = 60$ or an equivalent equation in the correct order with the denominators cleared; A1 for $x = 18$. A candidate with the correct order who writes $-4(x + 6)$ as $-4x + 24$ earns M1 A0. A candidate who subtracts in the wrong order, $\dfrac{x + 6}{3} - \dfrac{3x - 2}{4}$ (reaching $x = -6$), earns M0 A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 equations and inequalities: linear equations, including those with fractional coefficients, formed from a verbal statement. No quadratic, no algebraic denominators. Paper 1 opener, 2 marks: M1 for the correctly ordered equation with denominators cleared, A1 for $x = 18$.
question.originality_note: Not a re-skin of any real paper: GCE 2012 P1 Q8 and GCE 2023 P2 Q2(a) print the equation to be solved, while here the candidate must form it from the words, and the order of subtraction is the decision. Set 1 P1 Q1 formed an expression for a missing number from a mean; Set 1 P1 Q10 formed a linear equation from ratios of blends. This tests a different skill of linear equations: reading 'subtracted from' as reversed order, which forces a bracket with a negative sign in front, and the wrong order lands on the tidy but wrong $x = -6$.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both x = 18. Checked: (3(18)-2)/4 - (18+6)/3 = 13 - 8 = 5. The wrong order gives x = -6, an integer, so the trap lands on a tidy wrong answer.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on x = 18, and my own working confirms it.
fixes: Light edit, register only: the verbal 'is subtracted from ... the result is 5' reads as a lower-secondary textbook device. It is acceptable as a 2-mark opener; keep the reversed order, which is the point, and do not print the equation.

Mark scheme: M1 for 3(3x - 2) - 4(x + 6) = 60 (or an equivalent equation in the correct order with the denominators cleared), A1 for x = 18. A candidate with the right order who writes -4x + 24 earns M1 A0; one who subtracts in the stem's order (x = -6) earns M0 A0.
verdict.why: It is a 2-mark opener with one hidden reordering (the 2024/25 pattern for 2 marks) and a minus-bracket, the equation is formed by the candidate, and the wrong order gives the tidy x = -6. It is as demanding and as clean as Set 1 P1 Q1 or Q14. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2012 P1 Q8 or GCE 2023 P2 Q2(a), which print the equation, and it tests a different linear-equation skill from Set 1 P1 Q10.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 2 (mark scheme). Wording unchanged.

question.stem:
In triangle $PQR$, $PQ = 12$ cm, $PR = 7$ cm and angle $PQR = 30^\circ$.
Angle $PRQ$ is obtuse.
Calculate angle $QPR$.
skills: sine rule for an angle when two triangles fit the data, taking the obtuse angle as 180 degrees minus the calculator value
angle sum of the triangle to reach the angle that is asked for, which is not the one the sine rule gives
question.solution:
By the sine rule, $\dfrac{\sin PRQ}{PQ} = \dfrac{\sin PQR}{PR}$
$\sin PRQ = \dfrac{12 \sin 30^\circ}{7} = \dfrac{6}{7} = 0.85714\ldots$  (M1: $\sin PRQ = \dfrac{12 \sin 30^\circ}{7}$, or $\dfrac{6}{7}$)
The calculator gives $58.997^\circ$, but angle $PRQ$ is obtuse, so
angle $PRQ = 180^\circ - 58.997^\circ = 121.003^\circ$
Angle $QPR = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 121.003^\circ = 28.997^\circ = 29.0^\circ$ (to 1 d.p.)  (A1: $29.0^\circ$, which needs the obtuse angle $PRQ = 121.0^\circ$)
Check: $PR = 7$ lies between $PQ \sin 30^\circ = 6$ and $PQ = 12$, so two triangles fit the data; the statement that angle $PRQ$ is obtuse selects one of them.
Common error: using the acute value $59.0^\circ$ gives angle $QPR = 180^\circ - 30^\circ - 59.0^\circ = 91.0^\circ$ (tidy but wrong).
Mark scheme: M1 for $\sin PRQ = \dfrac{12 \sin 30^\circ}{7}$ $\left(= \dfrac{6}{7}\right)$; A1 for $29.0^\circ$, which needs the obtuse angle $PRQ = 121.0^\circ$. A candidate who uses the acute value $59.0^\circ$ and reaches $91.0^\circ$ scores M1 A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry: sine rule for any triangle, sine of an obtuse angle ($\sin(180^\circ - A) = \sin A$), angle sum of a triangle. The obtuse case given in the stem is set in real 4052-style papers (GCE 2020 P2 Q4, 'angle $ADC$ is obtuse'). No figure: a figure would show which angle is obtuse and remove the decision. 2 marks: M1 for $\sin PRQ = \dfrac{12 \sin 30^\circ}{7}$, A1 for $29.0^\circ$ (which needs the obtuse $121.0^\circ$).
question.originality_note: The real exemplars at this weight are equations such as $\sin(2x^\circ) = 0.561$ (GCE 2024 P1 Q20) and $\sin x^\circ = 0.9301$ (GCE 2023 P1 Q2); this is a triangle, not an equation, and it asks for the third angle so the sine-rule step is not named. GCE 2020 P2 Q4 used an obtuse angle as one step of a bearing chain in a park; nothing of that situation or its numbers is reused. Set 1 found a pentagon diagonal by the cosine rule (P1 Q20), formed a quadratic from $\frac12 ab \sin C$ (P1 Q23) and used trigonometry in solids, circles and a tunnel; none of them used the sine rule to find an angle or the obtuse case. The acute value leads to the tidy but wrong $91.0^\circ$.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 29.0 degrees. sin PRQ = 12 sin 30 / 7 = 6/7, calculator 58.997, obtuse PRQ = 121.003, QPR = 180 - 30 - 121.003 = 28.997 = 29.0. Two triangles fit because 6 < 7 < 12, and 30 + 121.0 < 180, so the obtuse case exists. The acute value gives the tidy wrong 91.0.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 29.0 degrees, and my own working confirms it; the obtuse configuration is valid.
fixes: Mark scheme: the setter's M1 ('sine rule and the obtuse angle chosen') would give the 91.0 candidate nothing, which contradicts the common-error line. Write it as M1 for sin PRQ = 12 sin 30 / 7 (= 6/7), and A1 for 29.0, which needs the obtuse 121.0. The acute-angle candidate then scores M1 A0.

Light edit, optional: SEAB sets this case with a diagram marked 'not drawn to scale' as well as the words 'angle ... is obtuse' (GCE 2020 P2 Q4). The paper may add a sketch that does not settle the angle by eye; taking 180 degrees minus the calculator value is still required either way. Leaving the question diagram-free is also acceptable.
verdict.why: One twist inside a routine rule: the calculator gives the acute angle, and the candidate must take its supplement and then use the angle sum for an angle the sine rule does not give. This matches the demand of GCE 2024 P1 Q20 [2], and the wrong decision lands on the believable 91.0. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2023 P1 Q2 or GCE 2024 P1 Q20, which are equations and not triangles. No earlier Set used the sine rule for an angle or the obtuse case (Set 1 P1 Q20 and Q23 use the cosine rule and the area formula), and it is as clean as Set 1's 2-mark questions.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (mark scheme). No diagram (fix 2 left).

question.stem:
Last year, $60\%$ of the visitors to a museum were local visitors and the rest were overseas visitors.
This year, the number of local visitors is $10\%$ less than last year and the number of overseas visitors is $25\%$ more than last year.
The museum had $156\,000$ visitors this year.
Find the number of local visitors the museum had this year.
skills: combine a percentage decrease on one part and a percentage increase on the other part into the percentage change of the whole
reverse percentage from this year's total to last year's total, then a percentage of a percentage for the part
question.solution:
Let the number of visitors last year be $T$.
Local visitors last year $= 0.6T$; this year $= 0.9 \times 0.6T = 0.54T$.
Overseas visitors last year $= 0.4T$; this year $= 1.25 \times 0.4T = 0.5T$.
Total this year $= 0.54T + 0.5T = 1.04T$  (M1)
$1.04T = 156\,000$, so $T = 150\,000$  (M1)
Local visitors this year $= 0.54 \times 150\,000 = 81\,000$  (A1)
Check: local $90\,000 \to 81\,000$, overseas $60\,000 \to 75\,000$, total $156\,000$.
Common errors: assuming local visitors are still $60\%$ of the total gives $0.6 \times 156\,000 = 93\,600$ (tidy but wrong); averaging the two changes as a $7.5\%$ increase gives a total last year of $145\,116.3\ldots$, which is not a whole number.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 percentage: percentage increase and decrease, percentage of a percentage and reverse percentage. No other topic is needed. 3 marks: M1 for the whole as $1.04$ of last year (or $0.54T + 0.5T$), M1 for last year's total $150\,000$, A1 for $81\,000$.
question.originality_note: GCE 2025 P1 Q14 reverses a chain of successive changes to one quantity over three years; here two parts of one whole change by different percentages at the same time, and the candidate must see that the whole changes by $4\%$, not by the average of $-10\%$ and $+25\%$. GCE 2023 P1 Q7(b) takes a percentage of the remainder; GCE 2017 P1 Q7 asks how many adults must join a club to reach a target percentage; neither is this structure or context. Set 1 P1 Q3 was hire purchase with a total $10\%$ above the cash price, and Set 1 P2 Q2 a profit-then-loss chain on one bicycle; this is a different skill of percentage (the weighted change of a whole from changes in its parts) in a different situation. The tempting wrong assumption that the local share stays at $60\%$ lands on the tidy $93\,600$.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 81 000. 0.9(0.6T) + 1.25(0.4T) = 1.04T = 156 000, so T = 150 000 and the local visitors this year are 0.54 x 150 000 = 81 000. Check: 90 000 becomes 81 000 and 60 000 becomes 75 000, a total of 156 000. The trap 0.6 x 156 000 = 93 600 is tidy but wrong.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 81 000, and my own working confirms it.
verdict.why: At 3 marks there is one decision followed by a two-step routine, as the 2024/25 standard asks. The candidate must see that the whole changes by 4% (the weighted change, not the average and not 60% of this year's total), then reverse the percentage and take a percentage of a percentage. The numbers are exact, the stem does not name the method, and the tempting 93 600 is believable. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2025 P1 Q14, which is successive changes to one quantity, or of GCE 2023 P1 Q7(b), which is a percentage of a remainder. It does not repeat Set 1 P1 Q3 (a hire-purchase equation in the cash price) or Set 1 P2 Q2 (a profit-then-loss chain), and it matches Set 1 P1 Q3 for demand.

question.stem:
Buses on three routes leave a bus interchange at regular intervals.
Route A buses leave every 18 minutes, Route B buses leave every 12 minutes and Route C buses leave every $n$ minutes, where $n$ is a whole number.
Buses on all three routes leave together at 7.20 a.m.
The next time that buses on all three routes leave together is 1.20 p.m.
Find the smallest possible value of $n$.
skills: turn the next time three periodic departures coincide into an LCM of 360 minutes and work backwards to the unknown interval
find the smallest number that supplies the prime powers missing from the LCM of the known intervals (2^3 and 5), rather than dividing 360 by 36
question.solution:
From 7.20 a.m. to 1.20 p.m. is 6 hours $= 360$ minutes, so the LCM of 18, 12 and $n$ is 360.
$18 = 2 \times 3^2$ and $12 = 2^2 \times 3$, so the LCM of 18 and 12 is $2^2 \times 3^2 = 36$.
$360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$. [B1: $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ seen with the LCM of 18 and 12, $36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$]
The factors $2^3$ and $5$ do not come from 18 or 12, so $n$ must contain $2^3$ and $5$; it need not contain a factor 3.
Smallest $n = 2^3 \times 5 = 40$. [B1: $n = 40$]
Check: the LCM of 18, 12 and 40 is $2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 360$ minutes after 7.20 a.m., i.e. 1.20 p.m.
(The tempting answer $360 \div 36 = 10$ is wrong: the LCM of 36 and 10 is 180, so the buses would all leave together at 10.20 a.m. The possible values of $n$ are 40, 120 and 360.)
Mark scheme: B1 for $360 = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 5$ seen with the LCM of 18 and 12 ($36 = 2^2 \times 3^2$); B1 for $n = 40$. A candidate who reaches these factorisations and then answers $360 \div 36 = 10$ scores B1 B0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Numbers and their operations: prime factorisation and LCM, applied to a timing problem; conversion of hours to minutes. No content outside the syllabus.
question.originality_note: Reverses the classic 'when do they next coincide' LCM problem: the coincidence time is given and the unknown interval is found, with 'smallest possible' forcing the prime-power argument. Unlike GCE 2024 P1 Q19 (N from a given HCF and LCM), GCE 2021 P1 Q20 (two numbers from HCF and LCM), GCE 2003/2008 lightships (next time together) and Set 1 P1 Q19 (smallest number from remainders, LCM minus 3). New context, numbers and structure. The departure times (7.20 a.m. and 1.20 p.m.) are chosen so as not to echo the 6 00 a.m. start of GCE 2003 P1 Q6.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give n = 40. 6 hours = 360 minutes = LCM(18, 12, n). 18 and 12 supply only 2^2 x 3^2 = 36, so n must carry the 2^3 and the 5 of 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5, and it need not carry a 3. The values of n that work are 40, 120 and 360 (checked by enumeration), so the smallest is 40. The tempting 360 / 36 = 10 gives LCM 180, so the buses would meet at 9.00 a.m. The word 'next' is what rules it out.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on n = 40, and my own working (and a check of every n up to 400) confirms it.
fixes: Light edit: 'leave together at 6.00 a.m.' echoes GCE 2003 P1 Q6 ('flash simultaneously at 6 00 a.m.'). Move the times, for example 7.20 a.m. and 1.20 p.m. This keeps the 360-minute gap and the answer 40.

Mark scheme: the setter's M1 ('n must contain 2^3 and 5') gives a candidate who stops at 10 nothing, even when their working is correct up to that point. Use B1 for 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5 seen with the LCM of 18 and 12 (36 = 2^2 x 3^2), then B1 for n = 40. The candidate who answers 10 then scores B1 B0.
verdict.why: A 2-mark question with one hidden reversal, as the 2024/25 standard asks. The coincidence time is given and the interval is unknown, and 'smallest possible' makes the candidate reason with prime powers instead of dividing, which gives the believable wrong answer 10. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2003 P1 Q6 (the forward problem) or GCE 2024 P1 Q19 (abstract, with N fixed by both HCF and LCM). It tests a different LCM skill from Set 1 P1 Q19 (remainders, LCM minus 3), and it is as demanding and as clean as Set 1's 2-mark questions (P1 Q2, Q14, Q17).
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (times moved to 7.20 a.m. / 1.20 p.m., answer still 40) and fix 2 (mark scheme). Gates re-run.

question.stem: Express as a single fraction in its simplest form $\dfrac{x - 6}{x^2 - 4} + \dfrac{5}{x^2 + x - 6}$.
skills: factorise two different quadratic denominators (a difference of two squares and a trinomial) to find their lowest common denominator
factorise the quadratic numerator obtained to reveal and cancel the factor shared with the denominator
question.solution:
$x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2)$ and $x^2 + x - 6 = (x + 3)(x - 2)$, so the common denominator is $(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)$. [B1: both denominators factorised, with the LCD $(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)$]
$\dfrac{x - 6}{x^2 - 4} + \dfrac{5}{x^2 + x - 6} = \dfrac{(x - 6)(x + 3) + 5(x + 2)}{(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ [M1: combined numerator $(x - 6)(x + 3) + 5(x + 2)$]
$= \dfrac{x^2 - 3x - 18 + 5x + 10}{(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)}$
$= \dfrac{x^2 + 2x - 8}{(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)}$
$= \dfrac{(x + 4)(x - 2)}{(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)}$
$= \dfrac{x + 4}{(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ [A1: $\dfrac{x + 4}{(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ or $\dfrac{x + 4}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$]
(Also accept $\dfrac{x + 4}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$. An answer left as $\dfrac{x^2 + 2x - 8}{(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ is not in its simplest form.)
Mark scheme: B1 for both denominators factorised with the LCD $(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)$; M1 for the combined numerator $(x - 6)(x + 3) + 5(x + 2)$ over that denominator; A1 for $\dfrac{x + 4}{(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ or $\dfrac{x + 4}{x^2 + 5x + 6}$. An answer that stops at $\dfrac{x^2 + 2x - 8}{(x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)}$ scores B1 M1 A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Algebraic expressions: factorisation of quadratic expressions and a difference of two squares; addition of algebraic fractions with quadratic denominators; simplification. No content outside the syllabus.
question.originality_note: Two fractions whose denominators are both unfactorised quadratics with one shared linear factor, and whose combined numerator is a quadratic that must itself be factorised before it cancels. Differs from Set 1 P1 Q11 (solving an equation, rejecting a root), Set 1 P2 Q1(c) (three fractions with x, x - 1 and (x - 1)^2 denominators, no cancellation), GCE 2025 P2 Q1(d) (denominators given factorised, linear numerator collapses) and GCE 2024 P1 Q5 (numerical denominators).

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give (x + 4)/((x + 2)(x + 3)). Checked: x^2 - 4 = (x - 2)(x + 2) and x^2 + x - 6 = (x + 3)(x - 2), so the LCD is (x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3). The numerator is (x - 6)(x + 3) + 5(x + 2) = x^2 + 2x - 8 = (x + 4)(x - 2), and cancelling (x - 2) gives the key. Confirmed symbolically.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on (x + 4)/((x + 2)(x + 3)), and my own working confirms it.
fixes: Topic tags: add 'Algebra (Factorization)'. Three factorisations (both denominators and the numerator) are the whole demand, so the question fuses two topics as Set 1's short questions do. It should be tagged that way.

Mark scheme: B1 for both denominators factorised with the LCD (x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3); M1 for the combined numerator (x - 6)(x + 3) + 5(x + 2); A1 for (x + 4)/((x + 2)(x + 3)) or (x + 4)/(x^2 + 5x + 6). An answer that stops at (x^2 + 2x - 8)/((x - 2)(x + 2)(x + 3)) scores B1 M1 A0, as the setter says.

Whole Set (for the session, not a reason to reject this slot): 'Express as a single fraction in its simplest form' was also asked in Set 1 P2 Q1(c). This question tests a different sub-skill, an LCD from two factorised quadratics followed by a hidden cancellation, so it passes. This Set's P2 Q1 should therefore not carry another combine-into-one-fraction part. It should test a fraction equation or a rearrangement instead.
verdict.why: The twist is in the routine. Both denominators are unfactorised and share one factor, and the combined numerator must itself be factorised before the shared (x - 2) cancels. The candidate who stops early gets a tidy-looking but unfinished answer, and SEAB puts the A1 in exactly this place (GCE 2025 P2 Q1(d)). It is harder than GCE 2025 P2 Q1(d), where the denominators are given factorised, and at least as hard as GCE 2024 P1 Q5 or Q24. It matches Set 1 P1 Q15 (a pure-algebra 3-mark question with one twist) for demand and cleanliness. It is not a re-skin of any exemplar, and it is not a repeat of Set 1 P2 Q1(c) (a repeated factor, no cancellation) or of Set 1 P1 Q11 (solving an equation, rejecting a value).
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (Algebra (Factorization) tag added) and fix 2 (mark scheme). Fix 3 noted for P2 Q1 (no combine-into-one-fraction part there).

question.stem:
A fountain sends a jet of water from a nozzle at ground level on horizontal ground.
The height, $y$ metres, of the jet above the ground at a horizontal distance of $x$ metres from the nozzle is given by $y = ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants.
The jet hits the ground at a horizontal distance of 8 m from the nozzle.
At a horizontal distance of 1 m from the nozzle, the jet is 1.4 m above the ground.
Find the greatest height of the jet above the ground.
skills: use the two ground-level points of a parabolic path as the roots to write the quadratic in factorised form and find the constant from one further point
locate the maximum on the line of symmetry midway between the roots (or by completing the square) and evaluate it
question.solution:
The nozzle is at ground level, so $y = 0$ when $x = 0$; hence $c = 0$.
The jet hits the ground where $x = 8$, so the roots are $x = 0$ and $x = 8$ and $y = ax(x - 8)$. [M1: both ground points used, i.e. $c = 0$ with $64a + 8b = 0$, or $y = ax(x - 8)$]
When $x = 1$, $y = 1.4$: $a(1)(1 - 8) = 1.4$, so $-7a = 1.4$ and $a = -0.2$. [M1: $a = -0.2$ (and $b = 1.6$) from the point $(1, 1.4)$]
So $y = -0.2x(x - 8) = -0.2x^2 + 1.6x$.
The line of symmetry is midway between the roots, $x = 4$.
Greatest height $= -0.2(4)(4 - 8) = 3.2$ m. [A1: 3.2 m]
(Alternatively, with $c = 0$: $64a + 8b = 0$ and $a + b = 1.4$ give $a = -0.2$ and $b = 1.6$; completing the square, $y = -0.2(x^2 - 8x) = -0.2(x - 4)^2 + 3.2$, so the greatest height is 3.2 m.)
Mark scheme: M1 for using both ground points, i.e. $c = 0$ with $64a + 8b = 0$, or $y = ax(x - 8)$; M1 for $a = -0.2$ (and $b = 1.6$) from the point $(1, 1.4)$; A1 for 3.2 m. The first M1 is the separating mark: a candidate who writes equations in three unknowns from only the two stated conditions, without using $(0, 0)$ from the nozzle at ground level, cannot go on.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Functions and graphs: quadratic functions in factorised and completed-square form, roots, line of symmetry and maximum point, in a real-world context; no plotting and no calculus needed.
question.originality_note: No earlier Set has a quadratic-graph question. Unlike GCE 2025 P1 Q15 (b and c read from a sketch's roots and intercept), GCE 2025 P1 Q19 / 2020 P1 Q10 (completing the square on a given expression) and GCE 2018 P1 Q21 (a and b from two given points), here the candidate turns a physical description (nozzle at ground level, landing point, one height) into the roots and a point, builds the curve and finds its maximum from the symmetry. New context, numbers and structure.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 3.2 m. The nozzle at ground level gives (0, 0) and the landing point gives (8, 0), so y = ax(x - 8). At x = 1, -7a = 1.4, so a = -0.2 (b = 1.6, c = 0). The maximum is on x = 4: y = -0.2(4)(-4) = 3.2. Checked symbolically. The initial gradient is 1.6, so the jet leaves at about 58 degrees, which is physically sensible.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on 3.2 m, and my own working confirms it.
fixes: Light edit, register: the stem runs six lines, and Set 1 keeps a partless stem to 2–5 lines in which every sentence carries a fact. Drop 'in a park' and join 'The ground is horizontal.' to the first sentence ('... from a nozzle at ground level on horizontal ground.'). Keep the physical wording 'at ground level'. It is the whole idea, so never replace it with 'passes through the origin'.

Mark scheme: M1 for using both ground points, i.e. c = 0 with 64a + 8b = 0, or y = ax(x - 8); M1 for a = -0.2 (and b = 1.6) from the point (1, 1.4); A1 for 3.2 m. A candidate who writes three unknowns from only two conditions and does not use (0, 0) cannot go on. That is the separating mark, and the scheme should say so.
verdict.why: One decision and then a two-step routine, as the 2024/25 standard asks for 3 marks. The candidate must see that a nozzle at ground level and the landing point are the two roots, since nothing in the stem names a point or the factorised form. Then a comes from one further point, and the maximum is found on the line of symmetry. The core step of writing the curve from its roots and one point is shared with GCE 2025 P1 Q15(b), but here the roots are hidden in the context and the question asks for the maximum, so it is not a re-skin. No earlier Set has a quadratic-graph question, and it is as clean and as demanding for its marks as Set 1 P1 Q24 (a model from two conditions, then evaluated).
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (stem shortened, "at ground level" kept) and fix 2 (mark scheme).

question.stem: In this question, use ruler and compasses only and show all your construction arcs clearly.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Construct the rectangle $ABCD$ in which $AB = 10$ cm and $AD = 4$ cm.
parts.answer: Rectangle $ABCD$ with $AB = DC = 10$ cm and $AD = BC = 4$ cm, the right angle at $A$ (or $B$) constructed with compass arcs and $C$ fixed by arcs.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The point $P$ lies on the side $DC$ and angle $APB = 90^\circ$.
Construct the two possible positions of $P$ and label them $P_1$ and $P_2$.
Measure the distance $P_1P_2$.
parts.answer: $P_1$ and $P_2$ are where the circle on $AB$ as diameter (centre $M$, the midpoint of $AB$, radius 5 cm) cuts $DC$, 2 cm from $D$ and 2 cm from $C$; $P_1P_2 = 6.0$ cm (accept 5.8 cm to 6.2 cm).

question.answer: (a) Rectangle constructed with a compass right angle. (b) $P_1$, $P_2$ on the circle with diameter $AB$; $P_1P_2 = 6.0$ cm.
skills: construct a right angle at a point on a line with compasses to build a rectangle from two sides
turn the condition angle APB = 90 degrees into the circle on AB as diameter (angle in a semicircle)
locate both points where that circle cuts the opposite side and measure the distance between them
question.solution:
(a) Draw $AB = 10$ cm and produce $BA$ beyond $A$. With centre $A$, draw an arc cutting the line on both sides of $A$ at $X$ and $Y$. With centres $X$ and $Y$ and equal radii, draw arcs meeting at $Z$; then $AZ$ is perpendicular to $AB$. Mark $D$ on $AZ$ with $AD = 4$ cm. With centre $D$ and radius 10 cm, and with centre $B$ and radius 4 cm, draw arcs meeting at $C$ on the same side of $AB$ as $D$. Join $DC$ and $BC$.
(b) Angle $APB = 90^\circ$, so $AB$ subtends a right angle at $P$: $P$ lies on the circle with $AB$ as diameter (angle in a semicircle).
Construct the perpendicular bisector of $AB$; it meets $AB$ at its midpoint $M$, with $MA = MB = 5$ cm, and meets $DC$ at $N$, the midpoint of $DC$, with $MN = 4$ cm. (The midpoint $M$ may instead be found by measuring 5 cm along $AB$ with the ruler.)
With centre $M$ and radius 5 cm, draw the circle (or arcs) cutting $DC$ at $P_1$ and $P_2$.
Check by calculation: in right-angled triangle $MNP_1$, $NP_1 = \sqrt{5^2 - 4^2} = 3$ cm, and likewise $NP_2 = 3$ cm, so $P_1$ is 2 cm from $D$, $P_2$ is 2 cm from $C$ and $P_1P_2 = 6$ cm.
Measured: $P_1P_2 = 6.0$ cm (accept 5.8 cm to 6.2 cm).
Tempting wrong answer: taking $P$ at the midpoint $N$ of $DC$, where angle $APB$ is obtuse, not $90^\circ$.
Mark scheme: (a) B1 a right angle at $A$ (or $B$) constructed with correct arcs; B1 rectangle completed with $AB = 10$ cm, $AD = 4$ cm, $C$ fixed by arcs. (b) B1 circle, or arcs, with centre $M$, the midpoint of $AB$, and radius 5 cm, cutting $DC$; accept $M$ found by the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ or by measuring 5 cm along $AB$ with the ruler. B1 both $P_1$ and $P_2$ marked on $DC$ with $P_1P_2 = 6.0$ cm (5.8 to 6.2). A candidate who instead calculates $x^2 - 10x + 16 = 0$ (with $DP = x$), and then marks the points 2 cm from $D$ and 2 cm from $C$ by measuring, scores B0 for the circle and B1 for both points with $P_1P_2 = 6.0$ cm, because the question asks for the positions to be constructed.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Geometry and Measurement: construction of simple geometrical figures from given data using ruler and compasses (a perpendicular at a point on a line, a perpendicular bisector, a circle of given centre and radius) and properties of circles (the angle in a semicircle is a right angle). No protractor, no loci beyond circles and bisectors, nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: New situation and structure: a rectangle built from two sides with a compass right angle, then the two points on the opposite side that see AB at a right angle, found as the circle on AB as diameter. Set 1 P1 Q7 built a triangle from three sides and intersected a perpendicular bisector with an angle bisector; the real exemplars (GCE 2025 P1 Q7, 2023 specimen, 2019 P1 Q12, 2017 P1 Q10, 2011 P1 Q20) all bisect sides or angles of a printed figure and shade a region. No earlier question uses the angle-in-a-semicircle locus or asks for two positions.

answers.(a): Rectangle ABCD constructed: AB = 10 cm, perpendiculars constructed at A and B, AD = BC = 4 cm marked with compasses, D joined to C (check: diagonal AC = BD = sqrt(116) ≈ 10.8 cm)
answers.(b): P1 and P2 are where the circle with diameter AB (centre = midpoint M of AB, found by the perpendicular bisector of AB; radius 5 cm) cuts DC; DP1 = 2 cm, DP2 = 8 cm (so CP2 = 2 cm); P1P2 = 6 cm (±0.1 cm)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give rectangle ABCD with AB = DC = 10 cm and AD = BC = 4 cm, the right angle made with compass arcs and C fixed by arcs. The blind examiner's check, diagonal sqrt(116) = 10.8 cm, is consistent.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both put P1 and P2 where the circle on AB as diameter (centre M, the midpoint of AB, radius 5 cm) cuts DC, with P1P2 = 6 cm. Checked: DC is 4 cm from AB, so NP = sqrt(5^2 - 4^2) = 3 on each side of the midpoint N of DC. P1 is 2 cm from D, P2 is 2 cm from C, and P1P2 = 6.0 cm. Equivalently, with DP = x, x^2 + 16 + (10 - x)^2 + 16 = 100 gives x^2 - 10x + 16 = 0, so x = 2 or 8.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree in both parts, and my own working confirms P1P2 = 6 cm (2 cm from D and 2 cm from C).
fixes: Light edit: print the side AB = 10 cm in the answer space ('The side AB has been drawn', as GCE 2011 P1 Q20 does), so that the 10 cm by 4 cm rectangle is placed where the answer space allows. The two marks in (a) stay on the compass right angle at A (or B) and on fixing C with arcs.

Mark scheme, (b) first B1: accept M found by measuring 5 cm along AB with the ruler (the stem allows a ruler) as well as M found by the perpendicular bisector. The mark is for the circle, or arcs, with centre M and radius 5 cm cutting DC. As written, 'the constructed midpoint' would refuse a valid method the question does not forbid.

Mark scheme, (b) second B1: say what a candidate who calculates x^2 - 10x + 16 = 0 and then marks the points 2 cm from D and C by measuring receives. Suggested: B0 for the circle and B1 for both points with P1P2 = 6.0 cm, because the question asks for the positions to be constructed.
verdict.why: The idea carries half the marks. Turning 'angle APB = 90 degrees' into the circle on AB as diameter is not named in the stem and is less signposted than Set 1 P1 Q7's 'same distance from A as from B'. The compass-only right angle is the one twist in the 2-mark opener. The question joins constructions to circle properties, the 3-4-5 numbers give exactly 6 cm, and 'two possible positions' makes the candidate find both. It is not a re-skin of any real construction question: GCE 2025 P1 Q7, the 2023 specimen, GCE 2019 P1 Q12 and GCE 2017 P1 Q10 bisect a printed figure and shade a region. It shares only the generic build, locate, measure shape with Set 1 P1 Q7, and tests different skills from it (a right angle and the angle-in-a-semicircle locus, not an SSS triangle and the meeting point of two bisectors).
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fixes 2 and 3 (mark scheme). Fix 1 left: the construction stays self-contained.

question.stem:
The first four terms of a sequence are shown below.
$\dfrac{1}{3} \qquad \dfrac{3}{7} \qquad \dfrac{5}{11} \qquad \dfrac{7}{15}$
Find the first term of the sequence that is greater than $0.495$.
Give your answer as a fraction.
You must show your working.
skills: general term of a sequence of fractions whose numerators and denominators are two separate linear sequences, found without a prompt
turn 'the first term greater than 0.495' into a linear inequality in n and take the least whole number above the non-integer bound 25.25
give the term itself, not its position, and reject the 25th term 49/99 that rounds to 0.495
question.solution:
Numerators $1, 3, 5, 7, \ldots$: the $n$th numerator is $2n - 1$.
Denominators $3, 7, 11, 15, \ldots$: the $n$th denominator is $4n - 1$.
So the $n$th term is $\dfrac{2n-1}{4n-1}$.
For the term to be greater than $0.495$: $\dfrac{2n-1}{4n-1} > 0.495$.
Since $4n - 1 > 0$,
$2n - 1 > 0.495(4n - 1) = 1.98n - 0.495$
$0.02n > 0.505$
$n > 25.25$
The least whole number is $n = 26$, so the first such term is the 26th term, $\dfrac{2(26)-1}{4(26)-1} = \dfrac{51}{103}$ $(= 0.49514\ldots)$.
Check: the 25th term is $\dfrac{49}{99} = 0.49494\ldots$, which is less than $0.495$ ($49 \times 200 = 9800 < 9801 = 99 \times 99$).
Tempting wrong answers: rounding $n > 25.25$ down to $n = 25$ gives $\dfrac{49}{99}$, which shows as $0.495$ correct to 3 significant figures but is not greater than $0.495$; giving $n = 26$ instead of the term. Listing the terms one at a time would need 26 terms, so the inequality is the working the question expects.
Mark scheme: B1 the $n$th term $\dfrac{2n-1}{4n-1}$ seen or used. M1 the inequality (or the equation) $\dfrac{2n-1}{4n-1} > 0.495$ solved to $n > 25.25$ (or $n = 25.25$). A1 $\dfrac{51}{103}$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Number and Algebra: number patterns (recognising a pattern and finding the nth term of a sequence whose numerators and denominators are linear sequences) and linear inequalities in one unknown (solving, then the least integer). No quadratic inequality, no limits, nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: One 3-mark question with no parts and no explain part: the candidate forms the nth term of a sequence of fractions unprompted, turns 'the first term greater than 0.495' into a linear inequality, takes the least whole number and gives the term. The threshold is set 26 terms out so that listing terms is not a sensible route. Set 1 P1 Q25 found the nth term of a quadratic integer sequence, solved an EQUATION for the term number and explained a parity fact; this tests a different skill (an inequality, the least integer above a non-integer bound, a fraction sequence) with no explain mark. The exemplars (GCE 2024 P1 Q8, 2023 P1 Q25, 2023 P2 Q8, 2020 P1 Q11, 2012 P1 Q7) are integer sequences asking for terms, an nth term or a term number from an equation; none uses an inequality. The paper's other inequality question, Q15, is a double inequality from three price plans; this is an inequality in a term number.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter and blind examiner both give 51/103. Checked exactly: the nth term is (2n - 1)/(4n - 1), and 200(2n - 1) > 99(4n - 1) gives 4n > 101, so n > 25.25 and n = 26. T25 = 49/99 = 0.49494... is not greater than 0.495 and T26 = 51/103 = 0.49514... is. The sequence increases towards 1/2, so the first term past 0.495 is well defined.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 51/103, and my own exact check (T25 = 49/99 below 0.495, T26 = 51/103 above it) confirms the key.
fixes: Wording, to SEAB's register: open with 'The first four terms of a sequence are shown below.' The printed terms already show they are fractions, so 'of fractions' is not needed.
Wording: end with 'You must show your working.', as in GCE 2024 P1 Q14, in place of 'Show your working.'. Keep 'Give your answer as a fraction.', since that line stops the answers 26 and 0.495.
verdict.why: It is one 3-mark question with nothing named in the stem. The candidate forms the nth term of a fraction sequence and turns 'first term greater than 0.495' into an inequality, which is the twist item 4 names. They then take the least whole number above 25.25 and give the term itself. The threshold is 26 terms out, so listing is not a sensible route, and the wrong decision to round down lands on 49/99, which shows as 0.495. That is as demanding for its marks as Set 1's 3-mark questions (P1 Q19 and Q16), and it is a different skill from Set 1 P1 Q25, which solved an equation for a term number in an integer quadratic sequence and ended with an explain-odd part.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish (after the round-2 verdict): fixes 1 and 2 (wording only).

question.stem:
$A$ and $B$ are points on a circle, centre $O$.
The length of the minor arc $AB$ is $5\pi$ cm and the area of the minor sector $AOB$ is $30\pi$ cm$^2$.
Find angle $AOB$, giving your answer in degrees.
skills: find the unknown radius by eliminating the angle between the arc-length and sector-area formulas (sector area = half the radius times the arc length)
convert an exact angle given in terms of pi radians into degrees
question.solution:
Let the radius be $r$ cm and angle $AOB = \theta$ radians.
Arc length: $r\theta = 5\pi$.
Area of sector: $\dfrac{1}{2}r^2\theta = 30\pi$.
Dividing the second equation by the first: $\dfrac{1}{2}r = \dfrac{30\pi}{5\pi} = 6$, so $r = 12$.
(Equivalently, area of sector $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times r \times \text{arc length}$: $30\pi = \dfrac{1}{2} \times r \times 5\pi$, so $r = 12$.)
$\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ radians.
(Or eliminate $r$ first: $r = \dfrac{5\pi}{\theta}$, so $\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{\theta}\right)^2\theta = \dfrac{25\pi^2}{2\theta} = 30\pi$, which gives $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ radians directly.)
Angle $AOB = \dfrac{5\pi}{12} \times \dfrac{180^\circ}{\pi} = 75^\circ$.
In degrees throughout: $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r = 5\pi$ gives $\theta r = 900$, and $\dfrac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 = 30\pi$ gives $\theta r^2 = 10\,800$, so $r = 12$ and $\theta = 75$.
Check: arc $= 12 \times \dfrac{5\pi}{12} = 5\pi$; area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 144 \times \dfrac{5\pi}{12} = 30\pi$.
Tempting wrong answers: dropping the $\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $r = 6$, $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $150^\circ$; stopping at $\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ (or $1.31$) radians leaves the angle unconverted.
Mark scheme: M1 $r = 12$ (from the two formulas, or area $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times r \times$ arc), or $\theta = \dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ radians (or 1.31 radians) reached by eliminating $r$ first, or $\theta r = 900$ and $\theta r^2 = 10\,800$ in degrees; A1 $75^\circ$. $150^\circ$ scores M0 A0; $\dfrac{5\pi}{12}$ radians scores M1 A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Geometry and Measurement: arc length and sector area with the angle in radians (or degrees), conversion between radians and degrees. No calculus, no trigonometric identities; nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: New skill for our Sets: two unknowns (the radius and the angle) fixed by the arc length and the sector area together, the radius found by eliminating the angle, then an exact radian angle converted to degrees. Set 1 P1 Q2 scaled a sector by an area factor and added two radii for a perimeter; Set 1 P2 Q8 found a radius from a chord and a height and took a major arc. No chord, no reflex angle and no perimeter here. GCE 2006 P1 Q15 gives the whole circle's area (the radius at once) and subtracts arcs; GCE 2015 P2 Q5(b), GCE 2019 P2 Q6(b) and GCE 2010 P2 Q8 work back from a perimeter; GCE 2016 specimen P2 Q8(b) finds an angle from an area with the radius given; GCE 2023 P1 Q2(b) converts a decimal radian angle alone.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 75°. My check: area = ½ × r × arc gives 30π = ½ × r × 5π, so r = 12. Then θ = 5π/12 rad = 75°, which is under 180°, so the arc is the minor arc as stated. The degree route is just as clean: θr = 900 and θr² = 10 800 give r = 12 and θ = 75. Arc 12 × 5π/12 = 5π and area ½ × 144 × 5π/12 = 30π both check.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on 75°, and my own working confirms it by both the radian route and the degree route.
fixes: Mark scheme: also give M1 for θ = 5π/12 rad (or 1.31 rad) reached by eliminating r first. That route substitutes r = 5π/θ into ½r²θ = 30π, which gives 25π/(2θ) = 30π. The scheme should not look only for r = 12. 5π/12 left in radians stays M1 A0, as the setter wrote.
Optional wording edit, in SEAB's register: 'Find angle AOB, giving your answer in degrees.' Two lines ('Find angle AOB.' then 'Give your answer in degrees.') is also acceptable.
verdict.why: At 2 marks this is one hidden step on a routine, as the real 2024/25 papers set it (compare GCE 2025 P1 Q9, a cube's volume from its surface area). The stem gives neither the radius nor the angle, so the candidate has to see that two formulas must be combined to remove one unknown, and then convert the angle to degrees. The numbers are clean, and dropping the ½ gives a believable wrong answer of 150°. Beside Set 1 P1 Q2 (scale a sector by an area factor, then a perimeter) it asks as much for its marks and tests a different Circular Measure skill. It does not repeat Set 1 P2 Q8, whose angle came from a chord and a height, and it does not re-skin any 2024/25 question. The skills the setter named are accurate and specific.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish (after the round-2 verdict): fixes 1 (mark scheme) and 2 (wording).

question.stem:
The line $l$ passes through the points $(-6, 10)$ and $(2, 6)$.
The line $m$ has equation $3x - 2y = 2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the area of the triangle enclosed by $l$, $m$ and the $y$-axis.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The lines $l$ and $m$ intersect at $P$. They meet the $y$-axis at $Q$ and $R$ respectively.
$S$ is the point such that $PQSR$ is a parallelogram.
Find the coordinates of $S$.

skills: equation of a line through two points, neither on the $y$-axis, formed unprompted because its $y$-intercept is a vertex of the triangle
area of the triangle cut off by two intersecting lines and the $y$-axis: base between the two $y$-intercepts, height the $x$-coordinate (not the $y$-coordinate) of their intersection
fourth vertex of a parallelogram read from the order of its named vertices, by translating a vertex by a side vector
question.solution:
(a) Gradient of $l = \frac{6 - 10}{2 - (-6)} = \frac{-4}{8} = -\frac{1}{2}$.
$l$: $y = -\frac{1}{2}x + c$ passes through $(2, 6)$, so $6 = -1 + c$ and $c = 7$.
$l$ is $y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 7$, so $l$ meets the $y$-axis at $(0, 7)$.   [M1: equation of $l$, or its $y$-intercept 7]
$m$: $3x - 2y = 2$ gives $2y = 3x - 2$, so $y = \frac{3}{2}x - 1$, and $m$ meets the $y$-axis at $(0, -1)$.
At the intersection of $l$ and $m$: $\frac{3}{2}x - 1 = -\frac{1}{2}x + 7$
$2x = 8$, so $x = 4$ and $y = \frac{3}{2}(4) - 1 = 5$. The lines meet at $(4, 5)$.   [M1: intersection, $x = 4$]
The triangle has vertices $(0, 7)$, $(0, -1)$ and $(4, 5)$. Take its base along the $y$-axis: $7 - (-1) = 8$ units. Its height is the horizontal distance from $(4, 5)$ to the $y$-axis, $4$ units.
Area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 4 = 16$ units$^2$.   [A1: $16$ units$^2$]
Tempting wrong answers: using the $y$-coordinate 5 as the height gives $\frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 5 = 20$ units$^2$; taking the base as $7 - 1 = 6$ gives $\frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 4 = 12$ units$^2$.
(b) $P$ is $(4, 5)$, $Q$ is $(0, 7)$ and $R$ is $(0, -1)$.
In the parallelogram $PQSR$ the side $PQ$ is opposite the side $RS$, so $\overrightarrow{RS} = \overrightarrow{PQ} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 - 4 \\ 7 - 5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$.
$S$ is $(0 - 4, -1 + 2) = (-4, 1)$.   [B1: $(-4, 1)$]
Check: $\overrightarrow{QS} = \begin{pmatrix} -4 \\ -6 \end{pmatrix} = \overrightarrow{PR}$, so the other pair of opposite sides is also parallel and equal.
Tempting wrong answer: taking the vertices in the order $P, Q, R, S$ gives $S = (4, -3)$.
Mark scheme: (a) M1 for the equation of $l$, $y = -\frac{1}{2}x + 7$, or its $y$-intercept 7; M1 for the intersection of $l$ and $m$, $x = 4$; A1 for $16$ units$^2$. Height 5 (giving 20) or base 6 (giving 12) scores M1 M1 A0. (b) B1 for $(-4, 1)$; $(4, -3)$ from the order $P, Q, R, S$ scores B0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 coordinate geometry: gradient of a line from two points, the equation $y = mx + c$, rearranging a given linear equation, solving two linear equations simultaneously, area of a triangle as $\frac{1}{2} \times$ base $\times$ height with the base on an axis; (b) uses a column-vector translation (4052 vectors: equal vectors for opposite sides of a parallelogram). No midpoint formula, no perpendicular-gradient rule, no shoelace formula is needed.
question.originality_note: Not Set 1 P2 Q6 (perpendicular gradients to place $C$ on $y = 9$, a perpendicular length, a ratio of triangle areas) and not the rejected equidistant-point draft: no point is fixed by a condition on two given points, no length or perpendicularity is used. Unlike GCE 2025 P2 Q8(a) (area of a trapezium bounded by $y = 2x + 1$, $x = p$ and the axes, given, leading to a quadratic in $p$) the area here is found, of a triangle bounded by two sloping lines and the $y$-axis, and the stem names neither the equation of $l$, nor the intersection, nor the vertices: the candidate must see that the base lies on the $y$-axis and the height is horizontal. Unlike GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q14 the equation of the line through two points is an unprompted step, not the question. The parallelogram part keeps the vertex-order sting the moderator asked to keep, on the new triangle. New numbers, new configuration. The line $m$, $3x - 2y = 2$, has gradient $\frac{3}{2}$, so $l$ and $m$ are not perpendicular: $PQSR$ is a parallelogram with no accidental right angle, and nothing echoes Set 1 P2 Q6's perpendicular gradients. (GCE 2025 P2 Q8(b)'s line $x - y = 2$ is not used.)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 20 units^2. Checked: gradient of l = -4/8 = -1/2, l is y = -x/2 + 7 (through (-6, 10) as well), m is y = 2x - 3, so they meet at (4, 5). The vertices are (0, 7), (0, -3) and (4, 5): base 10 on the y-axis, height 4, area 20. Three marks for the equation of l, the intersection and the area is dense next to the specimen's 3 marks for one equation, but it is within the 2024/25 P1 tariff and matches Set 1 P2 Q6(a) [3].

question.stem:
Kumar plays a game with a fair six-sided die, numbered 1 to 6.
He throws the die once.
If his first score is 6, he wins.
If it is 1 or 2, he loses.
If it is 3, 4 or 5, he throws the die again and wins only if his second score is greater than his first score.
Find the probability that Kumar wins the game.
skills: two-stage game in which the probability of success on the second throw depends on the score of the first throw
splitting into mutually exclusive branches by first score and adding the products
question.solution:
Win at the first throw: $P(6) = \frac{1}{6}$.   [B1]
Win at the second throw, by first score:
first score 3: second score 4, 5 or 6, probability $\frac{1}{6} \times \frac{3}{6} = \frac{3}{36}$
first score 4: second score 5 or 6, probability $\frac{1}{6} \times \frac{2}{6} = \frac{2}{36}$
first score 5: second score 6, probability $\frac{1}{6} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{36}$   [M1: a product for each first score, with the success probability changing with the first score]
P(Kumar wins) $= \frac{1}{6} + \frac{3}{36} + \frac{2}{36} + \frac{1}{36} = \frac{6}{36} + \frac{6}{36} = \frac{12}{36} = \frac{1}{3}$   [A1]
Tempting wrong answers: counting 'greater than or equal to' on the second throw gives $\frac{5}{12}$; treating the second throw as a win half of the time gives $\frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{12}$; using $P(\text{second} > \text{first}) = \frac{15}{36}$ for every first score gives $\frac{3}{8}$; leaving out the win on the first throw gives $\frac{1}{6}$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 probability: combined events by a possibility diagram or a tree diagram, independent throws of a fair die, adding mutually exclusive outcomes. No expectation, no conditional-probability notation, no more than two stages.
question.originality_note: Not Set 1 P1 Q13 (a quadratic in $n$ from a without-replacement probability, then 'exactly one') and not Set 1 P2 Q7(c) (two deliveries from a table): no unknown, no replacement question — the skill is a game whose second stage depends on the value of the first. Unlike GCE 2025 P1 Q27 (two spinners, unknown probabilities from products) and the GCE dice questions (totals or matching faces of several dice thrown together), the rules of the game decide which branches exist. New situation and structure.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both 1/3. Checked: 1/6 + (1/6)(3/6 + 2/6 + 1/6) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3. The tempting wrong answers check too: '>=' gives 5/12, and using 15/36 for every first score gives 3/8.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 1/3, and it checks exactly.
fixes: Light edit to SEAB register: write the rules one outcome per sentence and drop 'and loses otherwise'. For example: 'If his first score is 6, he wins. If it is 1 or 2, he loses. If it is 3, 4 or 5, he throws the die again and wins only if his second score is greater than his first score.' 'Loses otherwise' is correct but reads as a school-made rule sheet.
verdict.why: At the 3-mark standard ('one decision, then a two-step routine'). The candidate must see that the chance of a win on the second throw changes with the first score, split into branches by first score, and add the products. No tree or possibility diagram is named, the rules of the game decide which branches exist, and the wrong decisions land on believable numbers (5/12, 3/8). It is a different skill from Set 1 P1 Q13 (a quadratic in n from a without-replacement probability) and Set 1 P2 Q7(c), matches their demand for its marks, and is new to the corpus.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (one outcome per sentence).

question.stem:
$a$ and $b$ are constants.
The expansion of $(x + a)(x^2 + bx + 16)$ has no term in $x^2$ and no term in $x$.
The constant term of the expansion is positive.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the value of $a$ and the value of $b$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Solve the equation $(x + a)(x^2 + bx + 16) = 9x^3$.

skills: set the $x^2$ and $x$ coefficients of an expanded linear-times-quadratic product to zero to find two constants, turning 'the constant term is positive' into $16a > 0$ to choose between $a = \pm 4$
solve an equation that looks cubic by using the collapsed expansion $x^3 + 64$
question.solution:
(a) $(x + a)(x^2 + bx + 16) = x^3 + bx^2 + 16x + ax^2 + abx + 16a = x^3 + (a + b)x^2 + (ab + 16)x + 16a$   [M1: expansion with terms collected]
No term in $x^2$: $a + b = 0$, so $b = -a$.
No term in $x$: $ab + 16 = 0$.   [M1: both coefficients set to zero]
$a(-a) + 16 = 0$
$a^2 = 16$
$a = 4$ or $a = -4$.
The constant term of the expansion is $16a$, and it is positive, so $16a > 0$ and $a > 0$. Hence $a = 4$ and $b = -4$.   [A1: $a = 4$, $b = -4$, with $a = -4$ rejected]
(b) With $a = 4$ and $b = -4$, $(x + 4)(x^2 - 4x + 16) = x^3 + 16a = x^3 + 64$.
$x^3 + 64 = 9x^3$
$8x^3 = 64$
$x^3 = 8$
$x = 2$   [B1]
Tempting wrong answer: ignoring the positive constant term and taking $a = -4$, $b = 4$ gives the expansion $x^3 - 64$ and then $x^3 = -8$, $x = -2$.
Mark scheme: (a) M1 for the expansion with the terms collected, $x^3 + (a + b)x^2 + (ab + 16)x + 16a$; M1 for both coefficients set to zero, $a + b = 0$ and $ab + 16 = 0$; A1 for $a = 4$ and $b = -4$, with $a = -4$ rejected because the constant term $16a$ is positive. Leaving both pairs, or giving $a = -4$, $b = 4$, scores M1 M1 A0. (b) B1 for $x = 2$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 algebraic expressions and formulae: expansion of the product of a linear and a quadratic expression and algebraic identities (equating coefficients); solving $a^2 = 16$ and $x^3 = 8$ (square and cube roots). No discriminant, no factor theorem, no cubic-solving technique beyond taking a cube root.
question.originality_note: Not Set 1 P1 Q12 (expand a squared bracket times a linear factor; make $x$ the subject after the $x^2$ terms cancel) and not Set 1 P1 Q8 (a rectangle's side difference from $(l - w)^2$). Unlike GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q8 (rearrange a fractional equation into a given cubic and read off $a$ and $b$) and GCE 2024 P1 Q22 (a plain expansion), the constants are fixed by missing terms, one sign is rejected by the candidate's own reading of 'the constant term is positive' ($16a > 0$), and the collapsed product is then used to solve an equation. New structure and numbers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both a = 4, b = -4. Checked: the expansion is x^3 + (a + b)x^2 + (ab + 16)x + 16a, so a + b = 0 and ab + 16 = 0, giving a^2 = 16; a > 0 gives a = 4, b = -4.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both x = 2. Checked: (x + 4)(x^2 - 4x + 16) = x^3 + 64, so 8x^3 = 64 and x = 2, the only real root (the other two roots are complex).

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on both parts and both answers check exactly.
fixes: Hand the sign decision to the candidate instead of printing it. Replace 'a > 0' with 'The constant term of the expansion is positive'. The candidate must then turn 16a > 0 into the choice a = 4 over a = -4, which puts the given information one step from what the routine wants, as Set 1 does. The stem stays the same length, and ignoring the condition still lands on the tidy wrong answer x = -2.
verdict.why: At standard for 4 marks. In (a) [3] the candidate turns 'no term in x^2 and no term in x' into two equations nobody names and solves them with a sign choice. In (b) [1] the candidate uses the collapsed expansion x^3 + 64 instead of attacking a cubic. The question is as demanding as Set 1 P1 Q12 and tests a different skill (equating coefficients and the sum-of-cubes collapse, not expand-then-rearrange), and it is not a re-skin of GCE 2024 P1 Q22 or GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q8.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 applied — "a > 0" replaced by "the constant term of the expansion is positive". Round-2 blind solve agrees: a = 4, b = -4, x = 2.

question.stem:
$A$, $B$ and $C$ are points on a circle, centre $O$.
The tangent to the circle at $A$ meets $CB$ produced at $T$.
Angle $ATB = 28^\circ$ and angle $ACB = 35^\circ$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Find angle $OAC$.
Give a reason for each step of your working.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Find angle $ABC$.
Give a reason for each step of your working.

skills: angle at the point of contact found from a triangle outside the circle, less the right angle between tangent and radius
isosceles triangle of radii to the angle at the centre, then halved to an angle at the circumference
question.figure_description: A circle with centre O, shown as a dot labelled O. Draw the circle with O at the origin and radius about 3.5 cm. A is the LOWEST point of the circle (polar angle 270 degrees). C is on the circle at polar angle 36 degrees (upper right). B is on the circle at polar angle 200 degrees (left side, a little below the level of O). The tangent to the circle at A is a horizontal straight line through A; draw it from about half a radius to the right of A leftwards to the point T, which lies on this tangent about 2.2 radii to the LEFT of A. Draw one straight line from T through B to C, so that T, B and C are collinear with B between T and C. Also draw the chord AC, the chord AB, and the radius OA (do NOT draw the radius OC — with it drawn, the 35° label would sit inside angle OCA). Mark angle ATB (at T, between TA and TB) with an arc and the label 28°, and angle ACB (at C, between CA and CB) with an arc and the label 35°. Label the points A, B, C, O and T. Do NOT mark any other angle: no right-angle symbol at A, no angle at O, no angle at B, no angle OAC or TAC, and no lengths. No shading.
question.solution:
(a) Angle $TAC = 180^\circ - 28^\circ - 35^\circ = 117^\circ$ (angle sum of triangle $ATC$; $T$, $B$, $C$ are collinear, so angle $ATC = 28^\circ$ and angle $ACT = 35^\circ$).
Angle $OAT = 90^\circ$ (tangent perpendicular to radius).
Angle $OAC = 117^\circ - 90^\circ = 27^\circ$.
[B1 for $27^\circ$ with both reasons: angle sum of triangle $ATC$ and tangent perpendicular to radius.]
(b) Angle $OCA = 27^\circ$ (base angles of isosceles triangle, $OA = OC$ are radii).
Angle $AOC = 180^\circ - 27^\circ - 27^\circ = 126^\circ$ (angle sum of triangle).   [B1: angle $AOC = 126^\circ$ with the isosceles-radii and angle-sum reasons]
Angle $ABC = \frac{1}{2} \times 126^\circ = 63^\circ$ (angle at centre $= 2 \times$ angle at circumference).   [B1: $63^\circ$ with the angle-at-centre reason]
Alternative route in (b), accepted: angle $TAB$ = angle $ACB = 35^\circ$ (alternate segment theorem), then angle $ABC$ = angle $ATB$ + angle $TAB = 28^\circ + 35^\circ = 63^\circ$ (exterior angle of triangle $ATB$, since $T$, $B$, $C$ are collinear). The alternate segment theorem is not in the 4052 syllabus and is not needed, but a correct, correctly reasoned value by this route earns both marks of (b).
Check: in triangle $ABC$, angle $BAC = 180^\circ - 63^\circ - 35^\circ = 82^\circ$, so angle $TAB = 117^\circ - 82^\circ = 35^\circ$ and angle $ABT = 180^\circ - 28^\circ - 35^\circ = 117^\circ = 180^\circ - 63^\circ$, consistent with $T$, $B$, $C$ collinear.
Common errors: in (a), writing angle $OAC = 90^\circ - 35^\circ$ or $90^\circ - 28^\circ$ instead of working at $A$ from triangle $ATC$; in (b), taking angle $ABC$ equal to angle $AOC$.
Mark scheme: (a) [1] B1 for $27^\circ$ with both reasons (angle sum of triangle $ATC$; tangent perpendicular to radius). (b) [2] B1 for angle $AOC = 126^\circ$ with the reasons (base angles of the isosceles triangle $OAC$, $OA = OC$ radii; angle sum of triangle); B1 for $63^\circ$ with the reason (angle at centre $= 2 \times$ angle at circumference). Also accept in (b) a correctly reasoned value by the alternate segment route: B1 for angle $TAB = 35^\circ$ (alternate segment theorem), B1 for $63^\circ$ (exterior angle of triangle $ATB$). $126^\circ$ given as angle $ABC$ scores B1 B0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Properties of circles: tangent perpendicular to radius, angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference; plus angle sum of a triangle and the isosceles triangle of two radii. The alternate segment theorem is NOT needed (it is not in 4052); every step uses a listed property. The mark scheme still accepts a correct, correctly reasoned value in (b) by that route. Marks: (a) [1] B1 for $27^\circ$ with both reasons; (b) [2] B1 angle $AOC = 126^\circ$, B1 $63^\circ$.
question.originality_note: The given angles are at T and C, outside the circle's own angles, so the candidate must find the angle at the point of contact from triangle ATC and see that it contains the tangent-radius right angle; (b) then goes through the isosceles triangle of radii to the angle at the centre. Not GCE 2024 P1 Q13 (diameter AOC, angle in a semicircle, 'not a tangent'), not GCE 2025 P1 Q16 (O, B, T collinear with the tangent at A), not GCE 2023 P2 Q5, not GCE 2020 P1 Q3 (tangent with a radius parallel to a chord). Set 1 used intersecting chords and angles in the same segment (P1 Q9) and the incircle's tangent-chord angle (P2 Q5); this uses neither. In this paper Q7 uses the angle in a semicircle and Q9 the reflex angle of a major arc; this question uses neither.

answers.(a): 27° (angle TAB = angle ACB = 35° (alternate segment theorem); angle TAC = 180° − 28° − 35° = 117° (angle sum of triangle TAC); angle OAT = 90° (tangent ⊥ radius); angle OAC = 117° − 90° = 27°)
answers.(b): 63° (angle ABC = angle ATB + angle TAB = 28° + 35° = 63°, exterior angle of triangle ATB; equivalently ½ × angle AOC = ½ × 126°, angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 27°. Checked: T, B and C are collinear, so in triangle ATC angle ATC = 28° and angle ACT = 35°, giving angle TAC = 117°. Angle OAT = 90° (tangent perpendicular to radius), so angle OAC = 117° - 90° = 27°. The blind examiner also quoted the alternate segment theorem (angle TAB = 35°), which is not in 4052, but that step is not needed and the answer is the same. I built the figure from the description (A at 270°, B at 200°, C at 36°, T where CB meets the tangent) and measured ATB = 28.0°, ACB = 35.0°, OAC = 27.0°, so the data are consistent.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both 63°. In-syllabus route: angle OCA = 27° (isosceles triangle, OA = OC), angle AOC = 126°, angle ABC = 63° (angle at centre = 2 × angle at circumference). The blind examiner's exterior-angle route (28° + 35°) needs the alternate segment theorem, but it gives the same value. Measured on the constructed figure: 63.0°.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on 27° and 63°. My working and a coordinate construction of the figure confirm both.
fixes: Re-mark: (b) gains a mark and becomes [2] (B1 angle AOC = 126° with the isosceles-radii and angle-sum reasons, B1 63° with the angle-at-centre reason). It is three reasoned steps, and SEAB gives three reasoned steps 2 marks (GCE 2024 P1 Q13(a)). A 1-mark part with 'Give a reason for each step' is normally one fact (GCE 2025 P1 Q16(a)). The question then carries 4 marks. If the slot must stay at 3, (a) loses the mark instead: (a) [1] B1 for 27° with both reasons, and (b) [2].

Mark scheme: a candidate who quotes the alternate segment theorem (angle TAB = 35°, then angle ABC = 28° + 35° by the exterior angle of triangle ATB) gets the right value by a method outside 4052. State whether that earns the (b) mark. The usual ruling is to accept a correct, correctly reasoned value.
verdict.why: At standard for 3 marks. Both given angles sit away from where the answer lives. In (a) the candidate must pick triangle ATC (using the collinearity to read angle ACT as 35°) and see that the obtuse angle at the point of contact contains the tangent-radius right angle. The tempting 90° - 35° = 55° or 90° - 28° = 62° is a believable wrong answer. It belongs to the same family as GCE 2025 P1 Q16 (a tangent at A meeting a line through B at T). It is not a re-skin: the line through T is a secant CBT, not OBT, so the triangle and the chain differ. It uses different circle properties from Set 1 P1 Q9 and Set 1 P2 Q5(c) and is as clean as Set 1's circle question. The only real flaw is that (b) is under-marked.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: re-marked (a)[1] (b)[2] within the plan-locked 3 marks; fix 2 (alternate segment route accepted if correctly reasoned). The session removed radius OC from the figure so the 35-degree mark reads only as angle ACB.

question.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, angle $ABC = 44^\circ$.
The bisector of angle $BAC$ meets $BC$ at $D$.
The line through $D$ parallel to $CA$ meets $AB$ at $E$.
Angle $ADE = 38^\circ$.
Find angle $ACB$.
skills: alternate angles across an angle bisector to recover the whole angle
angle sum of a triangle after a parallel-line step
question.solution:
Angle $DAC$ = angle $ADE = 38^\circ$ (alternate angles, $DE$ is parallel to $CA$).
Angle $BAC = 2 \times 38^\circ = 76^\circ$ ($AD$ bisects angle $BAC$).
Angle $ACB = 180^\circ - 76^\circ - 44^\circ = 60^\circ$ (angle sum of triangle $ABC$).
[M1 for angle $DAC = 38^\circ$ stated with the reason 'alternate angles', or for angle $BAC = 76^\circ$; A1 for $60^\circ$.]
[The tempting $98^\circ$ (angle $BAC$ taken as $38^\circ$) scores M0 A0 unless angle $DAC = 38^\circ$ is stated separately with its reason, which earns M1 A0.]
Check: angle $BAD = 38^\circ$ = angle $ADE$, so triangle $AED$ is isosceles with $EA = ED$; and angle $BDE = 180^\circ - 44^\circ - 38^\circ - 38^\circ = 60^\circ$ = angle $ACB$ (corresponding angles), so the given angles are consistent.
Common error: taking angle $BAC = 38^\circ$ (using the alternate angle but forgetting that $AD$ only bisects angle $BAC$) gives angle $ACB = 98^\circ$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Angles, triangles and polygons: alternate angles for parallel lines, angle bisector, angle sum of a triangle. No figure needed; the configuration is fully determined by the text (D on BC, E on AB).
question.originality_note: Text-only triangle in which the given angle sits across the bisector, so the candidate must pass it through a pair of alternate angles and double it before the angle sum applies. Not GCE 2025 P1 Q13 (two isosceles triangles on one base), not GCE 2024 P1 Q15 (trapezium with an angle ratio), not GCE 2023 P1 Q14 (point equidistant from three vertices), not GCE 2016 specimen P1 Q4 (angles read across two parallel lines). No earlier Set has an Angles question.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both 60°. Checked: DE is parallel to CA and AD is a transversal, so angle DAC = angle ADE = 38° (alternate angles). AD bisects angle BAC, so angle BAC = 76°, and angle ACB = 180° - 76° - 44° = 60°. The figure is consistent: angle BAD = 38° = angle ADE makes triangle AED isosceles, and angle BDE = angle ACB = 60° (corresponding angles). The configuration is fully fixed by the text: D lies on segment BC and E on segment AB.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on 60°, and my own working confirms it.
fixes: Mark scheme: M1 for angle DAC = 38° stated with 'alternate angles', or for angle BAC = 76°; A1 for 60°. The tempting 98° (angle BAC taken as 38°) scores M0 A0 unless angle DAC = 38° is stated separately.

Register, optional: SEAB usually prints an angle question with a figure marked 'not drawn to scale'. Text-only is acceptable, as GCE 2024 P1 Q15 shows, and here drawing the sketch is part of the demand. If a figure is added, mark only angle ABC = 44° and angle ADE = 38°, so the alternate-angle transfer stays the candidate's.
verdict.why: A 2-mark question with the one hidden step the 2024/25 floor asks for. The given angle sits at D, across the bisector. The candidate must carry it through alternate angles and double it before the angle sum applies. Forgetting to double gives the tidy wrong answer 98°. It sits at the drilled end, comparable to GCE 2020 P1 Q3 and lighter than the 3-mark GCE 2025 P1 Q13. It matches Set 1 P1 Q9 in weight (two facts chained, the given angle one step from the answer). No Set has tested Angles, and it does not re-skin any exemplar.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (mark scheme); the check line no longer mentions a figure (there is none).

question.stem:
A gym offers three monthly plans.
Plan A: $\$10$ for each visit.
Plan B: a fee of $\$k$ plus $\$4$ for each visit.
Plan C: $\$120$ for any number of visits.
For a member who visits the gym 9 times in a month, Plan B is the cheapest of the three plans.
For a member who visits the gym 20 times in a month, Plan C is the cheapest of the three plans.
Find the range of values of $k$.
skills: turning 'cheapest of three plans' into linear inequalities in an unknown fee
combining the conditions from two usage levels into one double inequality, discarding the comparison that does not bind
strict inequalities, because a plan that ties is not the cheapest
question.solution:
9 visits: Plan A costs $\$90$, Plan B costs $\$(k + 36)$, Plan C costs $\$120$.
Plan B is the cheapest, so $k + 36 < 90$ and $k + 36 < 120$, i.e. $k < 54$ and $k < 84$. Together: $k < 54$.
20 visits: Plan A costs $\$200$, Plan B costs $\$(k + 80)$, Plan C costs $\$120$.
Plan C is the cheapest, so $120 < k + 80$ (and $120 < 200$, which is true), i.e. $k > 40$.
Hence $40 < k < 54$.
[M1 for $k + 36 < 90$ or $k < 54$; M1 for $k + 80 > 120$ or $k > 40$; A1 for $40 < k < 54$ with both signs strict.]
[$40 \le k \le 54$ scores M1 M1 A0 (the A1 needs strict signs: at $k = 54$ Plans A and B tie at $\$90$ for 9 visits, and at $k = 40$ Plans B and C tie at $\$120$ for 20 visits). $40 < k < 84$ (comparing Plan B only with Plan C for 9 visits) scores M0 M1 A0.]
The inequalities are strict: if $k = 54$, Plans A and B both cost $\$90$ for 9 visits, and if $k = 40$, Plans B and C both cost $\$120$ for 20 visits, so Plan B (or Plan C) would not be the cheapest.
Check with $k = 45$: 9 visits: A $\$90$, B $\$81$, C $\$120$ (B cheapest); 20 visits: A $\$200$, B $\$125$, C $\$120$ (C cheapest).
Common errors: comparing Plan B only with Plan C for 9 visits gives $40 < k < 84$; using $\le$ gives $40 \le k \le 54$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Equations and inequalities: linear inequalities formed from a worded situation and combined into a double inequality; problems in real-world contexts (comparing charges). No quadratic inequality, no graph, no whole-number rounding.
question.originality_note: The unknown is the plan's FEE, not the number of visits: two usage levels each give inequalities in k, one comparison does not bind, and the answer is a strict double inequality in a parameter. Not GCE 2024 P2 Q1(a) or GCE 2025 P1 Q6 (bare double inequalities to solve), not GCE 2019 P1 Q9(b). Set 1 had no inequality question, and no earlier Set compares tariffs. In this paper Q8 solves one linear inequality in n and takes the least integer; this question has no integer rounding and asks for a range of a parameter instead.

issues: Minor: 'cheapest' is read as strictly cheaper than the other plans. A reading that allows a tie would give 40 <= k <= 54; the strict reading is the standard one.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both 40 < k < 54. Checked: for 9 visits A = $90, B = $(k + 36) and C = $120. B cheapest gives k < 54 and k < 84, and only k < 54 binds. For 20 visits A = $200, B = $(k + 80) and C = $120. C cheapest gives k > 40, and C < A holds anyway. A scan of k from 0 to 200 in steps of 0.1 confirms that exactly 40 < k < 54 works. The blind examiner flagged the tie reading. 'Plan B is the cheapest' excludes a tie, so the strict signs are right.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on 40 < k < 54. The strict reading of 'cheapest' is correct.
fixes: Mark scheme: say how the tie reading is treated. The A1 needs the strict signs (at k = 54, Plans A and B tie at $90; at k = 40, Plans B and C tie at $120), so 40 ≤ k ≤ 54 scores M1 M1 A0. Also say that 40 < k < 84 (comparing B only with C at 9 visits) scores M0 M1 A0. The blind examiner's note shows a marker will meet the ≤ answer.
verdict.why: At standard for 3 marks. The candidate forms every inequality: 'cheapest of three' means comparing against both other plans at each usage level and keeping the comparison that binds. Comparing B only with C at 9 visits gives the tidy wrong range 40 < k < 84. The context changes the maths: it decides which comparisons exist and makes the signs strict. The question is unparted and clean, with no named equation. No real or Set question compares tariffs with an unknown fee. It is a different inequality skill from Q8's least integer in this paper, and it is as demanding and as clean as Set 1's 3-mark questions (P1 Q3, Q19).
