question.stem:
An investment account pays compound interest at a fixed rate per year.
Money invested in this account doubles in value every 16 years.
Priya invests $\$5000$ in this account and makes no further deposits or withdrawals.
Calculate the value of her investment at the end of 40 years.
Give your answer correct to the nearest cent.
skills: compound growth over a non-whole number of doubling periods, using the fractional index $2^{2.5}$
yearly growth factor found from a doubling time instead of a stated rate ($k^{16} = 2$)
question.solution:
Let the value be multiplied by $k$ each year. Doubling every 16 years gives $k^{16} = 2$, so $k = 2^{\frac{1}{16}}$ (a rate of about $4.43\%$ per year).
Value at the end of 40 years $= 5000k^{40} = 5000 \times \left(2^{\frac{1}{16}}\right)^{40} = 5000 \times 2^{\frac{40}{16}} = 5000 \times 2^{2.5}$ [M1 for $2^{\frac{1}{16}}$ or 40 years $= 2.5$ doubling periods; M1 for $5000 \times 2^{2.5}$ oe]
$= 5000 \times 5.656854\ldots = 28\,284.271\ldots$
Value $= \$28\,284.27$ [A1] (exactly $\$20\,000\sqrt{2}$).
[A candidate who rounds the yearly rate to $4.43\%$ before raising to the 40th power reaches $5000 \times 1.0443^{40} = \$28\,312.69$ and scores M1 M1 A0. The demand for the nearest cent is what rewards the exact route through $2^{\frac{40}{16}}$, so it is kept.]
Alternative route: after 32 years the money has doubled twice, to $\$20\,000$. The last 8 years are half a doubling period, so the value is multiplied by $2^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{2}$, not by $1.5$: $20\,000 \times \sqrt{2} = \$28\,284.27$.
Tempting wrong answers: $\$30\,000$ (adding half of the growth for the last 8 years), $\$25\,000$ ($5000 \times 2 \times 2.5$) and $\$20\,000$ (ignoring the last 8 years) all treat the growth as additive rather than multiplicative.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 financial mathematics (compound interest) and indices (fractional indices, laws of indices). Solvable with a scientific calculator; no logarithms are needed because 40 years is a known multiple (2.5) of the doubling time.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q5 compared second-year interest under simple 3.5% and compound 4%; the real papers find a principal from total interest (GCE 2024 P1 Q16, GCE 2017 P1 Q13), a rate from a start and an end value (GCE 2020 P1 Q15), or a monthly-compounded value (GCE 2023 P1 Q5). Here no rate is given at all: the candidate must turn a doubling time into a growth factor and handle half a doubling period multiplicatively ($\sqrt{2}$), which none of those asks.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree: $28 284.27 (exactly $20 000 sqrt 2), verified independently.
fixes: Light wording edit to SEAB register: replace 'The value of any amount of money invested in this account doubles every 16 years.' with 'Money invested in this account doubles in value every 16 years.'

Mark scheme: note that a candidate who rounds the yearly rate to 4.43% before raising to the 40th power reaches about $28 312.69 and earns M1 M1 A0 - the nearest-cent demand is what rewards the exact 2^(40/16) route, so keep it and say so in the scheme.
verdict.why: No rate is given: the candidate must turn a doubling time into a multiplicative factor over 2.5 periods, and the additive slip lands on a believable $30 000, so the one idea carries the marks, as Set 1 P1 Q5's second-year-only idea does; it is a different skill from Set 1 P1 Q5 and Set 1 P2 Q4, and no 2024/25 interest question works from a doubling time.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (wording) and fix 2 (mark scheme note).

question.stem:
$\xi$ is the universal set. $A$ and $B$ are sets such that $A \cap B = A$.
$n(\xi) = 50$, $n(A) = 12$ and $n(B') = 21$.
Find

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: $n(A' \cap B)$,

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: $n(A \cup B')$.

skills: deduce the subset relation $A \subseteq B$ from $A \cap B = A$ and use it to count a region
use the subset structure again for a union: $A$ lies inside $B$, so $A$ and $B'$ are disjoint and $n(A \cup B') = n(A) + n(B')$
question.solution:
$A \cap B = A$ means that every element of $A$ is also an element of $B$, so $A \subseteq B$ (set $A$ lies entirely inside set $B$).
$n(B) = n(\xi) - n(B') = 50 - 21 = 29$.
The four regions of the Venn diagram are: $A \cap B$ (which is all of $A$) $= 12$; $A' \cap B = 29 - 12 = 17$; $A \cap B' = 0$; $A' \cap B' = 21$. Check: $12 + 17 + 0 + 21 = 50$.
(a) $n(A' \cap B) = n(B) - n(A) = 29 - 12 = 17$ [B1]
(b) Since $A \subseteq B$, no element of $A$ lies outside $B$, so $n(A \cap B') = 0$: the sets $A$ and $B'$ are disjoint.
$n(A \cup B') = n(A) + n(B') = 12 + 21 = 33$ [B1]
(Equivalently, $A \cup B'$ is everything except the region $A' \cap B$, so $n(A \cup B') = 50 - 17 = 33$.)
Common error: $21$, from reading $A \cup B'$ as $(A \cup B)'$, which is $B'$ here.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 set language and notation: intersection, union, complement, subsets, numbers of elements in regions of a Venn diagram. No figure is needed; the candidate may sketch one.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q17 asked for the smallest possible overlap and the largest possible 'neither' from three given sizes (a bounding argument). GCE 2024 P1 Q17 reads compound expressions off a printed Venn diagram and GCE 2023 P1 Q17 shades and describes regions. Here there is no diagram and nothing is stated as a subset: the relation is hidden in the equation $A \cap B = A$ and $B$ is given only through its complement, so the candidate must build the structure before counting.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 17: A cap B = A gives n(A cap B) = 12, n(B) = 50 - 21 = 29, so n(A' cap B) = 29 - 12 = 17.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both 38: A' cup B' = (A cap B)' = A', so n = 50 - 12 = 38.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 17 and 38; both verified.
fixes: Make part (b) use the subset structure rather than only n(A cap B) = 12: ask for n(A cup B') instead (= 12 + 21 = 33, which needs A and B' to be disjoint because A lies inside B). As written, (b) falls to De Morgan in one line, so both parts rest on the same single substitution n(A cap B) = n(A).

Skills phrase 2 should read 'union of complements as the complement of the intersection (De Morgan), A' cup B' = (A cap B)' = A'' - the question does not require the candidate to see that one set lies inside the other for (b).
verdict.why: A 2-mark Sets question in the weight of GCE 2024 P1 Q17, with the given information one step away from the routine (the subset hidden in A cap B = A, B given only through its complement); it tests a different skill from Set 1 P1 Q17's bounding argument, though its two parts lean on one shared idea where Set 1's needed one each.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 applied — (b) now asks for n(A u B') = 33. Round-3 blind solve on the new wording agrees: 17, 33.

question.stem:
An adult has 5.0 litres of blood.
Each cubic millimetre of this blood contains $5.0 \times 10^{6}$ red blood cells.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Calculate the total number of red blood cells in the adult's blood.
Give your answer in standard form.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Each red blood cell lasts for 120 days and is then replaced by a new red blood cell.
The total number of red blood cells in the adult's blood stays the same.
Calculate the average number of new red blood cells the adult's body makes each second.
Give your answer in standard form.

skills: convert a volume from litres to cubic millimetres ($1$ litre $= 10^{6}$ mm$^3$) inside a standard-form product
steady-state replacement rate: the whole population is replaced once per lifetime, so rate $=$ total $\div$ lifetime in seconds
question.solution:
(a) $1$ litre $= 1000$ cm$^3$ and $1$ cm$^3 = 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000$ mm$^3$, so $1$ litre $= 10^{6}$ mm$^3$.
Volume of blood $= 5.0 \times 10^{6}$ mm$^3$ [M1 for the conversion used]
Number of red blood cells $= (5.0 \times 10^{6}) \times (5.0 \times 10^{6}) = 25 \times 10^{12} = 2.5 \times 10^{13}$ [A1]
(Tempting wrong answers: $5000$ mm$^3$ gives $2.5 \times 10^{10}$; $5000$ cm$^3 = 50\,000$ mm$^3$ gives $2.5 \times 10^{11}$.)
(b) Every cell lasts 120 days and the total does not change, so in 120 days all $2.5 \times 10^{13}$ cells are replaced: $2.5 \times 10^{13}$ new cells are made every 120 days.
$120$ days $= 120 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 10\,368\,000$ s $= 1.0368 \times 10^{7}$ s
Average number made each second $= \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{13}}{1.0368 \times 10^{7}}$ [M1] $= 2\,411\,265.4\ldots = 2.41 \times 10^{6}$ [A1]
(Tempting wrong answers: $2.08 \times 10^{11}$ is the number made each day, $4.02 \times 10^{7}$ the number made each minute.)
question.syllabus_check: 4052 numbers: standard form $A \times 10^{n}$ with operations on numbers in standard form; rate (a quantity per unit time) with conversion of units (litres to cubic millimetres, days to seconds). The facts used (1 litre = 1000 cm$^3$, 1 cm = 10 mm) are standard knowledge.
question.originality_note: No earlier Set has a standard-form question. The real standard-form questions ask for notation (GCE 2024 P1 Q18), a population density or difference (GCE 2023 P2 Q1, GCE 2009 P1 Q21), a rate multiplied by a time (GCE 2013 P1 Q21(c)), or a mass of atoms (GCE 2004 P1 Q12). Here (a) hides a cubic unit conversion inside the product, and (b) runs the rate the other way: the candidate must model a constant population replaced once per lifetime and divide the total by that lifetime in seconds. The blood-cell context is new to the corpus and its answers are the real biological values (about 25 million million cells, about 2.4 million new cells each second).

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both 2.5 x 10^13: 5.0 litres = 5.0 x 10^6 mm^3, times 5.0 x 10^6 cells per mm^3.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both 2.41 x 10^6: 2.5 x 10^13 cells replaced every 120 days = 1.0368 x 10^7 s, giving 2 411 265.4... per second.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 2.5 x 10^13 and 2.41 x 10^6; both verified.
verdict.why: Each 2-mark part carries its own unnamed idea (the cubic conversion 1 litre = 10^6 mm^3, whose linear slip lands on a believable 2.5 x 10^10; the steady-state model that the whole count is replaced once per lifetime), and the context changes the maths; it matches Set 1 P1 Q21's [2, 2] build, with no earlier Set standard-form question and nothing in 2024/25 like it.

question.stem:
A train travels along a straight track from one station to the next station, which is 3 km away.
The train starts from rest and accelerates at a constant rate of $0.5$ m/s$^2$ until it reaches its maximum speed.
It travels at this maximum speed and then decelerates at a constant rate of $1$ m/s$^2$ until it stops at the next station.
The journey takes 3 minutes.
Find the maximum speed of the train, in metres per second.
skills: times of the accelerating and decelerating stages as maximum speed divided by the gradient, leaving the constant-speed time as $(180 - 3v)$ s
distance as the area of a trapezium-shaped speed-time graph with the maximum speed unknown, giving a hidden quadratic
rejecting the root for which accelerating and decelerating alone would outlast the whole journey
question.solution:
Let the maximum speed be $v$ m/s.
Units: $3$ km $= 3000$ m and $3$ minutes $= 180$ s.
On a speed-time graph the acceleration is the gradient, so
time accelerating $= \frac{v}{0.5} = 2v$ s and time decelerating $= \frac{v}{1} = v$ s.
Time at the maximum speed $= 180 - 2v - v = (180 - 3v)$ s.  [M1]
The speed-time graph is a trapezium with parallel sides $180$ s and $(180 - 3v)$ s and height $v$ m/s. The distance travelled is the area under the graph:
$\frac{1}{2}(180 + 180 - 3v)v = 3000$  [M1]
(or $\frac{1}{2} \times 2v \times v + v(180 - 3v) + \frac{1}{2} \times v \times v = 3000$)
$180v - 1.5v^2 = 3000$
$1.5v^2 - 180v + 3000 = 0$
$v^2 - 120v + 2000 = 0$
$(v - 20)(v - 100) = 0$
$v = 20$ or $v = 100$
If $v = 100$, the train would take $200$ s just to reach its maximum speed, which is longer than the whole journey of $180$ s (the time at the maximum speed, $180 - 300 = -120$ s, would be negative). So $v = 100$ is rejected.
Maximum speed $= 20$ m/s  [A1]
Check: the train accelerates for $40$ s ($\frac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 20 = 400$ m), travels at $20$ m/s for $120$ s ($2400$ m) and decelerates for $20$ s ($\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 20 = 200$ m): $400 + 2400 + 200 = 3000$ m in $40 + 120 + 20 = 180$ s.
Mark scheme: M1 for the stage times $2v$ and $v$, or the constant-speed time $180 - 3v$; M1 for an area equation in consistent units equal to $3000$; A1 for $20$ only (accept $72$ km/h if clearly equivalent, but the question asks for m/s). Keeping both $20$ and $100$ scores M1 M1 A0.
Common errors: keeping $v = 100$; working in km and minutes without converting; taking the time to reach $v$ as $0.5v$ instead of $\frac{v}{0.5}$; giving the average speed $\frac{3000}{180} = 16.7$ m/s.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 speed-time graphs: gradient as acceleration or deceleration, area under the graph as distance travelled; conversion of units (km to m, minutes to s); forming and solving a quadratic equation by factorisation and rejecting a root in context. No calculus, no suvat formulae beyond what the graph gives; the candidate sketches or pictures the three-stage speed-time graph from the words.
question.originality_note: Topic not tested in any earlier Set. Unlike GCE 2025 P1 Q22 and GCE 2021 P1 Q24 (two cyclists on one road, a linear equation from two areas), this is one vehicle with no graph printed: the stem gives only the two accelerations, the total time and the total distance, the candidate must turn the gradients into stage times in terms of the unknown maximum speed, and the area gives a quadratic whose larger root is rejected by the time available, not by its sign. GCE 2017 P1 Q5 and GCE 2012 P1 Q19 read a printed graph with its times marked; here nothing is marked and no variable is named.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 20 m/s. Stage times v/0.5 = 2v s and v/1 = v s, so the constant-speed time is (180 - 3v) s; the trapezium area 1/2(180 + 180 - 3v)v = 3000 gives v^2 - 120v + 2000 = 0, so v = 20 or 100. v = 100 is rejected because accelerating alone would take 200 s, longer than the 180 s journey. Check: 400 + 2400 + 200 = 3000 m in 40 + 120 + 20 = 180 s. Mark-scheme note only: drop the 'accept 72 km/h' line, since the question asks for metres per second; A1 is 20 m/s with 100 rejected.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 20 m/s, and my own working confirms it, including the rejection of 100.
verdict.why: An unparted 3-mark hidden model in the 2025 manner: the candidate turns two accelerations into stage times, forms the trapezium area as a quadratic and rejects the root the journey time rules out (one model plus one standard case split, about 4 minutes), with 100 and 16.7 as tidy wrong answers. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2025 P1 Q22 (two cyclists, times given, a linear equation) or GCE 2017 P1 Q5, no earlier Set has a speed-time question, and it matches Set 1 P1 Q13 and Q23(a), hidden quadratics at 3 marks, for demand and cleanliness.

question.stem:
Each interior angle of a polygon is either $140^\circ$ or $160^\circ$.
The polygon has three more interior angles of $160^\circ$ than interior angles of $140^\circ$.
Find the number of sides of the polygon.
skills: sum of the exterior angles of an irregular polygon whose interior angles take two sizes
forming a linear equation in the number of angles of one size and giving the total number of sides, not that count
question.solution:
Let the polygon have $k$ interior angles of $140^\circ$. Then it has $(k + 3)$ interior angles of $160^\circ$.
The exterior angle at a $140^\circ$ vertex is $180^\circ - 140^\circ = 40^\circ$ and at a $160^\circ$ vertex is $180^\circ - 160^\circ = 20^\circ$.  [M1]
The exterior angles of any polygon add up to $360^\circ$:
$40k + 20(k + 3) = 360$  [M1]
$60k + 60 = 360$
$k = 5$
Number of sides $= k + (k + 3) = 5 + 8 = 13$  [A1]
Alternative (interior angles): the polygon has $(2k + 3)$ sides, so
$140k + 160(k + 3) = (2k + 3 - 2) \times 180$
$300k + 480 = 360k + 180$
$k = 5$, giving $13$ sides.
Check: $5 \times 140^\circ + 8 \times 160^\circ = 700^\circ + 1280^\circ = 1980^\circ = (13 - 2) \times 180^\circ$.
Mark scheme: M1 for the exterior angles $40^\circ$ and $20^\circ$, or for the interior-angle sum $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$ with $n$ in terms of one unknown; M1 for a correct equation in one unknown; A1 for $13$.
Common errors: giving $5$ (the number of $140^\circ$ angles) or $8$ as the answer; using $(k - 2) \times 180^\circ$ with $k$ the number of one kind of angle only; treating the polygon as regular.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 angles of polygons: the sum of the exterior angles of any polygon is $360^\circ$ (equivalently the interior-angle sum $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$), interior and exterior angles on a straight line, and a linear equation formed from a worded condition. The polygon need not be regular; such a convex 13-sided polygon exists because every exterior angle is positive and they add up to $360^\circ$.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q20 found a regular pentagon's interior angle and then a diagonal by the cosine rule; this question uses no trigonometry and an irregular polygon, testing the exterior-angle sum with an unknown count. It differs from GCE 2021 P1 Q11 (a regular polygon from an interior:exterior ratio), GCE 2013 P2 Q7(a)(ii) (four known angles, the remaining angle in terms of n), GCE 2015 P1 Q16 and GCE 2006 P1 Q13 (a fixed number of sides with one unknown angle) and GCE 2018 P1 Q14 (regular polygons meeting at a point): here both angle sizes are known and it is the number of sides that is hidden, reached through an equation the candidate must set up.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 13. Exterior angles 40 and 20 degrees: 40k + 20(k + 3) = 360 gives k = 5, so there are 5 + 8 = 13 sides. Check: 5 x 140 + 8 x 160 = 1980 = 11 x 180. Believable wrong answers: 5 or 8 (one kind of angle only) and 12 (treating the polygon as regular with the average angle 150 degrees).

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 13 sides, and my own working confirms it.
verdict.why: One decision (use the exterior-angle sum, or the interior sum with n = 2k + 3, for a polygon that is not regular and whose counts are given only as a difference), then a two-step routine: the 3-mark shape of the 2024/25 standard, fusing polygons with a linear equation as Set 1's short questions do, with three tidy wrong answers (5, 8, 12). It is not a re-skin of GCE 2021 P1 Q11 or GCE 2017 P1 Q8 (regular polygons), it tests a different polygon skill from Set 1 P1 Q20 (a regular pentagon's diagonal by the cosine rule), and it is as clean and demanding as Set 1 P1 Q19 or Q20.

question.stem:
A flat has an air-conditioner, a water heater and a washing machine.
The matrix $\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} 6 & 10 \\ 0.5 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}$ shows the number of hours for which each appliance is used on a weekday and on a weekend day.
The rows represent the air-conditioner, the water heater and the washing machine, and the columns represent a weekday and a weekend day.
The power ratings of the air-conditioner, the water heater and the washing machine are $1.5$ kW, $3$ kW and $0.5$ kW respectively.
The electricity used by an appliance, in kilowatt-hours (kWh), is its power rating, in kW, multiplied by the number of hours for which it is used.
A week has 5 weekdays and 2 weekend days.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Write down a product of matrices whose single element is the total electricity, in kWh, used by the three appliances in one week, and evaluate it.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Electricity costs 30 cents per kWh.
The water heater is replaced by a new water heater with a different power rating. The number of hours for which each appliance is used does not change.
The cost of the electricity used by the three appliances in one week is now $\$26.55$.
Find the power rating of the new water heater.

skills: ordering a chain of three matrices so that the product has a single element: a $1 \times 3$ row of power ratings, the $3 \times 2$ hours matrix and a $2 \times 1$ column of the numbers of days
working back from a weekly electricity bill, weighting 5 weekdays and 2 weekend days, to an unknown entry of the power-rating matrix
question.solution:
(a) The rows of $\mathbf{H}$ are the appliances, so the power ratings must be written as a $1 \times 3$ row matrix in the same order, $\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 3 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, placed in front of $\mathbf{H}$.
The columns of $\mathbf{H}$ are a weekday and a weekend day, so the numbers of days in a week must be written as a $2 \times 1$ column matrix in the same order, $\mathbf{D} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$, placed after $\mathbf{H}$.
$\mathbf{PHD}$ is $1 \times 3$ times $3 \times 2$ times $2 \times 1$, which gives a $1 \times 1$ matrix: its single element is the total electricity, in kWh, used in one week.
$\begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 3 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 6 & 10 \\ 0.5 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}$  [M1 for this product in a defined order, or the equivalent product $\begin{pmatrix} 5 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 6 & 0.5 & 1 \\ 10 & 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1.5 \\ 3 \\ 0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ with the hours re-written as a $2 \times 3$ matrix]
$\begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 3 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}\mathbf{H} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.5 \times 6 + 3 \times 0.5 + 0.5 \times 1 & 1.5 \times 10 + 3 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 11 & 19 \end{pmatrix}$ (11 kWh on a weekday, 19 kWh on a weekend day).
$\begin{pmatrix} 11 & 19 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 55 + 38 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 93 \end{pmatrix}$  [A1]
(Multiplying $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{D}$ first gives the same result: $\mathbf{HD} = \begin{pmatrix} 50 \\ 4.5 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix} 1.5 & 3 & 0.5 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 50 \\ 4.5 \\ 9 \end{pmatrix} = (75 + 13.5 + 4.5) = (93)$.)
The three appliances use 93 kWh in one week.

(b) Let the power rating of the new water heater be $w$ kW.
Electricity on a weekday $= 1.5 \times 6 + 0.5w + 0.5 \times 1 = 9.5 + 0.5w$ kWh.
Electricity on a weekend day $= 1.5 \times 10 + 1 \times w + 0.5 \times 2 = 16 + w$ kWh.
Electricity in one week $= 5(9.5 + 0.5w) + 2(16 + w) = 79.5 + 4.5w$ kWh.
Cost: $0.30(79.5 + 4.5w) = 26.55$  [M1]
$79.5 + 4.5w = 88.5$
$w = 2$
Power rating of the new water heater $= 2$ kW  [A1]
Alternative: with the old heater, one week uses 93 kWh (part (a)), costing $93 \times \$0.30 = \$27.90$. The saving is $\$27.90 - \$26.55 = \$1.35$, which is $\frac{1.35}{0.30} = 4.5$ kWh. The water heater is used $5 \times 0.5 + 2 \times 1 = 4.5$ hours a week, so its power rating falls by $\frac{4.5}{4.5} = 1$ kW, from $3$ kW to $2$ kW.
Mark scheme: M1 for a correct equation in the new rating (or the saving of $4.5$ kWh set against the heater's $4.5$ hours a week) with both the weekday and the weekend weightings $5$ and $2$; A1 for $2$ kW.
Common errors in (a): attempting $\mathbf{HP}$ or $\mathbf{DH}$, or writing the ratings as a column and multiplying in either order (not defined); stopping at $\begin{pmatrix} 11 & 19 \end{pmatrix}$, which gives a weekday and a weekend day, not a week; using $\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$ for the days, which gives $(30)$, or $\begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{pmatrix}$ (the days in the wrong order), which gives $(117)$. Common errors in (b): treating a week as 7 weekdays, or as one weekday plus one weekend day; using the heater's hours on one kind of day only.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 matrices: display of information in a matrix, the order of a matrix, when a product of matrices is defined, multiplication of a $1 \times 3$ matrix by a $3 \times 2$ matrix and of the result by a $2 \times 1$ matrix (two products of two matrices), and interpretation of the elements of a product; rate (cents per kWh) and a utilities bill from 4052 financial mathematics; a linear equation. No inverse, determinant or transpose notation is required: the candidate chooses how to write the power ratings and the numbers of days as matrices.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q21 multiplied a sales matrix by a price-and-cost matrix whose order and shapes were printed, then compared the profit per meal on two days; its (a) found a matrix of per-day totals. Here (a) asks for a single element, the week's total: neither the row of power ratings nor the column of numbers of days is given as a matrix, so the candidate must form both and order a chain of three matrices (the ratings FIRST, because $\mathbf{H}$ times a row is not defined, and the days LAST). Part (b) then works backwards from a weekly bill to an unknown entry of the ratings row, rather than comparing two totals. It is not the SEAB pattern of GCE 2017 P1 Q19, GCE 2019 P1 Q21, GCE 2022 P1 Q18 and GCE 2023 P1 Q21 (an unknown x printed in a quantity matrix, the product in terms of x, then x from an equality of two elements): no product is named, no matrix is printed with x in it, and the condition is a bill for a week, not a comparison of two elements.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: The blind examiner wrote (11.5 19); the key's (11 19) is right: 1.5 x 6 + 3 x 0.5 + 0.5 x 1 = 9 + 1.5 + 0.5 = 11 and 1.5 x 10 + 3 x 1 + 0.5 x 2 = 15 + 3 + 1 = 19. The 11.5 is an arithmetic slip in the weekday element, not an ambiguity: H is stated clearly and only (1.5 3 0.5)H, or its transposed equivalent, can be formed.

parts.label: (b)

Check by the saving: the old week is 5 x 11 + 2 x 19 = 93 kWh = $27.90, the saving of $1.35 is 4.5 kWh, and the heater runs 4.5 hours a week, so its rating falls by 1 kW to 2 kW. Tidy wrong answer: 1 kW (the fall, not the new rating).

verdict.key_verdict: They differ only in (a), where the setter is right (11 kWh on a weekday, not 11.5) and the blind examiner made an arithmetic slip; the key is correct in both parts and the question is sound.

question.stem:
In a gymnastics competition, each judge on a panel gives each gymnast a mark.
A gymnast's score is the mean of the marks that remain when the highest mark and the lowest mark are left out.
For one gymnast, the highest mark is $9.6$ and the lowest mark is $7.8$.
When only the highest mark is left out, the mean of the remaining marks is $0.1$ less than the mean of all the marks.
When only the lowest mark is left out, the mean of the remaining marks is $0.2$ more than the mean of all the marks.
Find the gymnast's score.
skills: a mean recalculated with one value left out: the new total over one fewer value, with both the number of values and the mean unknown
two such conditions (highest left out, lowest left out) solved simultaneously for the number of values and their mean
a trimmed mean with both extremes left out, from the total and the count found
question.solution:
Let there be $n$ judges and let the mean of all the marks be $m$. The total of all the marks is $nm$.
Only the highest mark left out: $n - 1$ marks remain, with total $nm - 9.6$.
$\frac{nm - 9.6}{n - 1} = m - 0.1$
$nm - 9.6 = nm - 0.1n - m + 0.1$
$m + 0.1n = 9.7$ ... (1)
Only the lowest mark left out: $n - 1$ marks remain, with total $nm - 7.8$.
$\frac{nm - 7.8}{n - 1} = m + 0.2$
$nm - 7.8 = nm + 0.2n - m - 0.2$
$m - 0.2n = 7.6$ ... (2)
(1) $-$ (2): $0.3n = 2.1$, so $n = 7$, and $m = 9.7 - 0.7 = 9$.
Total of all the marks $= 7 \times 9 = 63$.
With both the highest and the lowest marks left out, $5$ marks remain, with total $63 - 9.6 - 7.8 = 45.6$.
Score $= \frac{45.6}{5} = 9.12$
Check: $\frac{63 - 9.6}{6} = 8.9 = 9 - 0.1$ and $\frac{63 - 7.8}{6} = 9.2 = 9 + 0.2$.
Marking: M1 one correct equation, e.g. $\frac{nm - 9.6}{n - 1} = m - 0.1$; M1 both equations reduced to linear form, $m + 0.1n = 9.7$ and $m - 0.2n = 7.6$ (or equivalent); A1 $n = 7$ and mean $9$; A1 score $9.12$.
Common errors: keeping the count at $n$ when a mark is left out, i.e. taking $9.6 - m = 0.1n$ and $m - 7.8 = 0.2n$, gives $6$ judges, mean $9$ and a tidy wrong score of $\frac{54 - 17.4}{4} = 9.15$; adding the two changes to the mean ($9 - 0.1 + 0.2$) gives $9.1$; dividing $45.6$ by $7$ instead of $5$ gives $6.51$, which is below the lowest mark.
question.syllabus_check: 4052: mean of ungrouped data (total = mean × number of values); expansion of a product of two linear expressions; simultaneous linear equations formed from a worded situation. All within the syllabus; the working needs no calculator but none is forbidden. The data are consistent: the other five marks total 45.6 (mean 9.12), which lies between 7.8 and 9.6.
question.originality_note: New situation and a new skill of the topic. Set 1 P1 Q14 was a bare pair; Set 1 P1 Q22 took two measurements (edge totals) of one solid with two unknown dimensions, and the rejected draft two border areas of one photograph — here nothing is measured twice: the two equations come from how a MEAN changes when one value is left out, and the unknowns are the number of values and their mean, not two lengths. The answer is neither unknown but the trimmed mean they give. Q25 of this paper finds an unknown frequency from the mean of a frequency table; this asks for the effect of removing an extreme value on a mean, twice, which Q25 does not. Set 1 P1 Q1 formed the fifth number from a mean and Set 1 P1 Q4 used a median of ages; neither is this. No real GCE paper in the corpus recalculates a mean with a value left out (searched).

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter and blind examiner both give 9.12. My own working agrees: with n judges and mean m, (nm - 9.6)/(n - 1) = m - 0.1 gives m + 0.1n = 9.7 and (nm - 7.8)/(n - 1) = m + 0.2 gives m - 0.2n = 7.6, so n = 7, m = 9, total 63. Checks: 53.4/6 = 8.9 and 55.2/6 = 9.2. The five middle marks total 45.6, so the score is 45.6/5 = 9.12 exactly, which lies between 7.8 and 9.6, so the data are consistent. A quicker route gives the same answer: leaving out one value x changes the mean by (x - m)/(n - 1), so 9.6 - m = 0.1(n - 1) and m - 7.8 = 0.2(n - 1). Adding them gives n - 1 = 6. A tie at the highest or lowest mark would not change any equation. The tempting wrong answer is confirmed: keeping the count at n gives n = 6, m = 9 and (54 - 17.4)/4 = 9.15.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 9.12, and my own working (by two routes) confirms it.
fixes: Light wording edit so the stem reads like SEAB. As printed, 'each judge on a panel gives a gymnast a mark' is followed by 'The highest mark given to one gymnast', which makes the reader stop to see which gymnast is meant. Suggested: 'In a gymnastics competition, each judge on a panel gives each gymnast a mark. A gymnast's score is the mean of the marks that remain when the highest mark and the lowest mark are left out. For one gymnast, the highest mark is 9.6 and the lowest mark is 7.8.' Keep the last three sentences as they are. This also brings the stem nearer the 2–5 lines Set 1 uses for a question with no parts.

For the session, no change to this slot: Q25(a) of this paper also turns a mean into a linear equation in which the count is unknown (k is in both the total and the number of students). The two are different skills: Q25(a) is the mean of a frequency table, and this question is how a mean changes when one value is left out, with the count and the mean both unknown. Both can stay, but the paper should not carry a third item that forms an equation from a mean with an unknown count.
verdict.why: The candidate introduces both unknowns (the number of judges and their mean), models the count dropping to n - 1 when one mark is left out, sees the nm term cancel, and then needs the count n - 2 for the score. That is one non-obvious idea followed by routine work, finishable in about 6 minutes, and keeping the count at n gives a tidy wrong answer of 9.15. Beside Set 1 P1 Q22 (wire edges of two solids, then the volume), it is as demanding, just as clean (n = 7, mean 9, score 9.12 exactly) and tests a different skill of simultaneous equations: it builds a mean-change model and does not take two measurements of one object. The previous moderator named this change of direction. No 2024/25 question is re-skinned; GCE 2024 P1 Q21 finds p from a mean over a known count.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish (after the round-2 verdict): fix 1 (stem wording). Fix 2 was a note for the session (no third mean-with-unknown-count item in the paper).

question.stem:
In triangle $PQR$, angle $QPR = 90^\circ$.
$S$ is the point on $QR$ such that $PS$ is perpendicular to $QR$.
The diagram is not drawn to scale.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
Show that triangle $PQS$ is similar to triangle $RPS$.
Give a reason for each statement you make.
parts.answer: Angle $PSQ$ = angle $RSP = 90^\circ$ ($PS$ perpendicular to $QR$). Angle $QPS = 90^\circ -$ angle $SPR$ (angle $QPR = 90^\circ$) and angle $PRS = 90^\circ -$ angle $SPR$ (angle sum of triangle $PSR$), so angle $QPS$ = angle $PRS$. Two pairs of equal angles, so triangle $PQS$ is similar to triangle $RPS$ (AA).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
$PS = 6$ cm and $SR$ is $5$ cm longer than $QS$.
Find the length of $QR$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find, in its simplest form, the ratio $PQ : PR$.

skills: prove the two triangles cut off by the perpendicular from the right angle similar, using a complementary-angle argument
pair corresponding sides correctly to get QS x SR = PS^2, form and solve a quadratic, reject the negative root
ratio of the two shorter sides of the big triangle read off as the scale factor of the similar triangles
question.figure_description: Triangle PQR with side QR horizontal along the bottom, Q at the left end and R at the right end. P is above QR and placed so that angle QPR is a right angle (mark it with a small square at P). S is the point on QR directly below P, joined to P by a vertical segment PS; mark the right angle at S with a small square. Draw to these proportions, which are deliberately NOT those of the answer: Q at (0, 0), S at (5, 0), R at (13, 0), P at (5, √40 ≈ 6.32), so S is between Q and R and nearer to Q, and angle QPR is still exactly a right angle (QS × SR = 5 × 8 = 40 = PS²). Label only the four points P, Q, R and S. Show NO lengths, NO angle sizes and no other markings (in particular do not write 6 cm, 13 cm, x or any ratio). Nothing the candidate is asked to find (QR, QS, SR, the ratio PQ : PR) appears on the figure.
question.solution:
(a) Angle $PSQ$ = angle $RSP = 90^\circ$ (given $PS$ is perpendicular to $QR$).
Angle $QPS$ + angle $SPR = 90^\circ$ (angle $QPR = 90^\circ$), so angle $QPS = 90^\circ -$ angle $SPR$.
In triangle $PSR$, angle $PRS = 180^\circ - 90^\circ -$ angle $SPR = 90^\circ -$ angle $SPR$ (angle sum of a triangle).
So angle $QPS$ = angle $PRS$.
Two pairs of corresponding angles are equal, so triangle $PQS$ is similar to triangle $RPS$ (AA), with $P \leftrightarrow R$, $Q \leftrightarrow P$, $S \leftrightarrow S$.
[B1 for one pair of equal angles with its reason: either angle $QPS$ = angle $PRS$ or angle $PQS$ = angle $RPS$ earns this mark; B1 for the right angles at $S$ and the AA conclusion, with the similarity stated in the order triangle $PQS$ similar to triangle $RPS$.]
(b) Let $QS = x$ cm, so $SR = (x + 5)$ cm.
From (a), $\frac{QS}{PS} = \frac{PS}{RS}$, so $\frac{x}{6} = \frac{6}{x + 5}$.
$x(x + 5) = 36 \Rightarrow x^2 + 5x - 36 = 0 \Rightarrow (x + 9)(x - 4) = 0$.
$x = 4$ or $x = -9$; a length cannot be negative, so $x = 4$.
$QS = 4$ cm, $SR = 9$ cm, so $QR = 4 + 9 = 13$ cm.
[M1 for $\frac{QS}{PS} = \frac{PS}{RS}$ in $x$, or for the Pythagoras route below to the same quadratic; M1 quadratic formed and solved; A1 $QR = 13$ cm, $-9$ rejected.]
(Alternative route: $PQ^2 = x^2 + 36$, $PR^2 = (x + 5)^2 + 36$, $PQ^2 + PR^2 = (2x + 5)^2$ gives the same $x^2 + 5x - 36 = 0$.)
(c) The scale factor from triangle $RPS$ to triangle $PQS$ is $\frac{QS}{PS} = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3}$.
$PQ$ and $RP$ are corresponding sides, so $\frac{PQ}{PR} = \frac{2}{3}$, i.e. $PQ : PR = 2 : 3$.
(Check: $PQ = \sqrt{52} = 7.21$ cm, $PR = \sqrt{117} = 10.8$ cm, and $\frac{7.211}{10.817} = 0.667$.)
Common error: $QS : SR = 4 : 9$, which is the ratio of the areas of the two triangles, not of the sides.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 congruence and similarity: AA test for similar triangles with reasons stated; ratio of corresponding sides; angle sum of a triangle; quadratic equation solved by factorisation with a root rejected. No circle theorems, no trigonometry, no surds needed (the ratio comes from the scale factor).
question.originality_note: The Set's similarity proof; Set 1 had only Q18 (a rectangle whose halves are similar to it). Not GCE 2025 P1 Q20 (two squares, congruent triangles, perimeters), not GCE 2021 P1 Q14 / GCE 2003 P1 Q21 / GCE 2011 P1 Q10 (the equal angle is GIVEN there; here it must be derived from the right angles), not GCE 2025 P2 Q4 (a common angle plus a right angle). The perpendicular from the right angle to the hypotenuse appears in GCE 2020 P1 Q22(a) only as a 1-mark step inside a field-area question with the equal angle given. Letters P, Q, R, S used so the wording does not echo Set 1 P1 Q23 (triangle ABC, sine-area formula, cosine rule).

answers.(a): shown — angle PSQ = angle RSP = 90° (PS perpendicular to QR); angle PQS = 90° − angle QPS (angle sum of triangle PQS) = angle RPS (since angle QPR = 90°); so triangle PQS is similar to triangle RPS (AA)
answers.(b): QR = 13 cm (QS = 4 cm, SR = 9 cm, from PS^2 = QS × SR: x(x+5) = 36, x = 4)

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both prove AA similarity with the correspondence P<->R, Q<->P, S<->S. The setter shows angle QPS = angle PRS (each is 90 degrees - angle SPR); the examiner shows angle PQS = angle RPS. Either is a valid equal-angle pair, alongside the two right angles at S.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give QR = 13 cm. Checked: from (a), QS/PS = PS/RS, so x(x + 5) = 36, x^2 + 5x - 36 = 0, (x + 9)(x - 4) = 0, x = 4 (reject -9); QS = 4, SR = 9, QR = 13. The Pythagoras route gives the same quadratic.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Both give 2 : 3. PQ corresponds to RP, and the scale factor is QS/PS = 4/6. Check: PQ = sqrt(52) = 2 sqrt(13), PR = sqrt(117) = 3 sqrt(13). The tempting wrong answer, 4 : 9 (QS : SR, which is PQ^2 : PR^2), is a believable number.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on every part (AA similarity, QR = 13 cm, PQ : PR = 2 : 3), and my own working confirms each.
fixes: The figure is drawn exactly to the answer (Q at 0, S at 4, R at 13, P at (4, 6)), so QS : PS : SR on the printed diagram is exactly 4 : 6 : 9. A candidate can measure PQ and PR and read off 2 : 3 for the 1-mark part (c), or check QR in (b). Draw it with other proportions that still keep angle QPR = 90 degrees, for example Q (0, 0), S (5, 0), R (13, 0), P (5, sqrt 40 = 6.32).

Mark scheme (a): state that either equal-angle pair (angle QPS = angle PRS, or angle PQS = angle RPS) earns the first B1 with its reason, and that the similarity statement must keep the order PQS ~ RPS. Mark scheme (b): M1 for QS/PS = PS/RS in x, or for the Pythagoras route to the same quadratic.
verdict.why: This is the 6-7-mark shape (i) in standard.md, like GCE 2025 P1 Q20 (a proof that yields a fact, a hidden quadratic that uses it, a 1-mark sting). The figure (similarity, not congruence) and the relation (PS^2 = QS x SR) are new, so it is not a re-skin. It gives the Set its geometric proof, which Set 1 lacked. Beside Set 1 P1 Q23 it is equally demanding: the idea in (b) is pairing the corresponding sides correctly, and (c) turns the result into a scale factor with 4 : 9 as the trap. Its only flaw is a diagram drawn to the exact answer proportions.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 2 (mark scheme) and fix 1 — "not drawn to scale" added and the figure redrawn with S at 5 and P at (5, sqrt 40), so the drawing no longer gives 4 : 6 : 9. Answers unchanged.

question.stem: Factorise completely $(x^2 + x)^2 - (x^2 + x) - 2$.
skills: treat the repeated quadratic expression $x^2 + x$ as a single variable and factorise the resulting quadratic
finish completely: factorise the quadratic factor that splits and recognise that $x^2 + x + 1$ does not factorise
question.solution:
Let $u = x^2 + x$. The expression is $u^2 - u - 2 = (u - 2)(u + 1)$.
So it equals $(x^2 + x - 2)(x^2 + x + 1)$.
$x^2 + x - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1)$.
$x^2 + x + 1$ does not factorise: no two integers have product $1$ and sum $1$ (its discriminant is $1^2 - 4(1)(1) = -3 < 0$, so it has no real roots).
Answer: $(x + 2)(x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)$ (factors in any order).
Check by expanding: both the original and the answer equal $x^4 + 2x^3 - x - 2$.
Marking: M1 for $(x^2 + x - 2)(x^2 + x + 1)$, whether or not $u$ is named (or for $(u - 2)(u + 1)$ with $u = x^2 + x$); M1 for $x^2 + x - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1)$; A1 for $(x + 2)(x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1)$ with $x^2 + x + 1$ left as it is.
A candidate who expands to the quartic $x^4 + 2x^3 - x - 2$ first and then factorises it correctly gets full marks.
Common errors: stopping at $(x^2 + x - 2)(x^2 + x + 1)$ (not complete); forcing $x^2 + x + 1$ into linear factors, such as $(x + 1)^2$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 factorisation of quadratic trinomials applied to a quadratic in a composite expression, and knowing when a quadratic trinomial does not factorise. No factor theorem or other A-Math technique is needed.
question.originality_note: Not Set 1 P1 Q15 (regroup four terms, difference of squares), Set 1 P1 Q11 (factorise and cancel in an equation) or Set 1 P2 Q1(a) (grouping with a sign change). GCE 2017 P1 Q14 disguised a LINEAR bracket (2y - 3) behind a 'Hence' part that factorised the quadratic first; here there is no ladder, the disguised expression is itself quadratic, and 'completely' means factorising one quadratic factor further and knowing to stop at the other, $x^2 + x + 1$, which does not factorise. The finish adds a decision to the trinomial factorising already tested in this paper's Q5: knowing where to stop.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give (2x + 1)(x - 1)(2x - 3)(x + 1). Checked: with u = 2x^2 - x, u^2 - 4u + 3 = (u - 1)(u - 3); 2x^2 - x - 1 = (2x + 1)(x - 1) and 2x^2 - x - 3 = (2x - 3)(x + 1). Both forms expand to 4x^4 - 4x^3 - 7x^2 + 4x + 3.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on (2x + 1)(x - 1)(2x - 3)(x + 1), and a symbolic factorisation confirms it.
fixes: The finishing routine (factorising non-monic trinomials) is already the routine of this paper's Q5. To give the finish its own small decision, choose the inner expression so that 'completely' means knowing where to stop. For example, (x^2 + x)^2 - (x^2 + x) - 2 = (x^2 + x - 2)(x^2 + x + 1) = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1), where the last factor does not factorise. As set, the question is acceptable.
Mark scheme: award the first M1 for (2x^2 - x - 1)(2x^2 - x - 3) whether or not u is named, and say that a candidate who expands to the quartic first and then factorises it correctly gets full marks.
verdict.why: A 3-mark question with one decision followed by a two-stage routine. The candidate must see the repeated 2x^2 - x as one quantity with no 'hence' ladder (GCE 2017 P1 Q14 printed that ladder). Two non-monic factorisations follow, and stopping at the two quadratics is the tempting incomplete answer. Set 1 P1 Q15 is also a bare 3-mark 'factorise completely', but it tests a different skill (regrouping, then a difference of two squares). This question is at least as demanding and just as clean.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 applied — the expression is now (x^2 + x)^2 - (x^2 + x) - 2 = (x + 2)(x - 1)(x^2 + x + 1); fix 2 (mark scheme). Round-3 blind solve agrees.

question.stem:
The table shows the number of times each student in a group visited the school library in one week.
$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Number of visits} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Number of students} & 4 & 7 & 9 & k & 5 & 3 \\ \hline \end{array}$

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The mean number of visits per student is $2.4$.
Find the value of $k$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
Wei Ming says, “The upper quartile of the number of visits is 3, so one quarter of the students in the group visited the library more than 3 times.”
Is he correct?
Show working to support your answer.
parts.answer: No. The upper quartile is 3 (the 30th and 31st values are both 3), but only $5 + 3 = 8$ of the 40 students (20%) visited more than 3 times, not 10 (one quarter); 12 students visited exactly 3 times.

question.answer: (a) $k = 12$  (b) No: only 8 of the 40 students (20%) visited more than 3 times, not 10, because 12 students visited exactly 3 times.
skills: unknown frequency found from the mean of a frequency table, with the unknown in both the total and the count
upper quartile of discrete data with repeated values: the number of values strictly above the quartile is not a quarter
question.solution:
(a) Number of students $= 4 + 7 + 9 + k + 5 + 3 = 28 + k$.
Total number of visits $= 0(4) + 1(7) + 2(9) + 3k + 4(5) + 5(3) = 60 + 3k$.
$\frac{60 + 3k}{28 + k} = 2.4$
$60 + 3k = 67.2 + 2.4k$
$0.6k = 7.2$
$k = 12$
(Dividing by 28 instead of $28 + k$ gives $k = 2.4$, which is not a whole number of students.)
[M1 for $\frac{60 + 3k}{28 + k} = 2.4$ (or an equivalent equation formed from the table); A1 for $k = 12$.]
(b) With $k = 12$ there are 40 students. Cumulative frequencies: 4, 11, 20, 32, 37, 40.
The upper quartile lies between the 30th and 31st values. The 21st to 32nd values are all 3, so the upper quartile is 3 and the first part of his statement is true.
Number of students who visited more than 3 times $= 5 + 3 = 8$, which is $\frac{8}{40} = 20\%$ of the students.
One quarter of the students would be $\frac{1}{4} \times 40 = 10$ students.
So he is not correct: 12 students visited exactly 3 times, and the upper quartile falls among them, so only 8 students (not 10) visited more than 3 times.
[B1 for 8 students (or $20\%$) visiting more than 3 times, which needs $k = 12$; B1 for 'No' with the comparison against 10 students (or $25\%$). A bare 'No', or 'Yes, because that is what the upper quartile means', earns 0.]
question.syllabus_check: 4052 data handling and analysis: mean of data in a frequency table; quartiles of ungrouped (discrete) data; interpreting a quartile in context. No grouped data, no formula beyond the mean.
question.originality_note: New situation (library visits, discrete frequency table with one unknown frequency). Set 1 P1 Q4 found a missing data value from a median of a list and re-inserted values; Set 1 P2 Q7 used a grouped cumulative table for mean/SD and a claim the grouped table cannot test. GCE 2024 P1 Q4(b) tested a proportion claim read from a box plot; here the claim is about ties in discrete data, where the count above the upper quartile (8) is not a quarter (10). GCE 2024 P1 Q21 found an unknown data value from a mean via a quadratic; here the unknown is a frequency and the equation is linear with the unknown in the total.

answers.(b): No. With k = 12 there are 40 students; the 30th and 31st values are both 3, so the upper quartile is 3 (that part is right). But only 5 + 3 = 8 students visited more than 3 times, which is 8/40 = 1/5 (20%), not one quarter (that would need 10 students). Many students visited exactly 3 times, so he is not correct.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give k = 12. (60 + 3k)/(28 + k) = 2.4 gives 0.6k = 7.2, so k = 12. Dividing by 28 instead of 28 + k gives k = 2.4, which is not a whole number, so this trap corrects itself.

parts.label: (b)

Optional, for a 5: (a) is the textbook form of the unknown-frequency item. Give its information one step away from the mean (a change in the mean, or the mean of part of the group), still leading to k = 12, so that (a) also needs a small idea and (b) is unchanged.

question.stem:
A cylindrical aquarium has internal radius 30 cm and internal height 60 cm.
Water flows into the aquarium through a pipe of internal diameter 3 cm at a speed of $0.4$ m/s.
The pipe is always full of water.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
The aquarium is empty.
Calculate the time taken to fill the aquarium completely.
Give your answer in minutes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The aquarium is emptied. A solid stone sphere of radius 15 cm is placed on the base of the aquarium.
Water flows into the aquarium again through the same pipe at the same speed.
Calculate the depth of the water in the aquarium 5 minutes after the water starts to flow.

skills: volume flow rate from a pipe's cross-sectional area and the water's speed, converting m/s to cm/s and diameter to radius
water depth in a cylinder holding a submerged solid: (water volume + solid volume) divided by the base area, checked against the height of the solid
question.solution:
(a) Radius of pipe $= 1.5$ cm and speed $= 0.4$ m/s $= 40$ cm/s.
Volume of water flowing in each second $= \pi (1.5)^2 \times 40 = 90\pi$ cm$^3$.
Capacity of the aquarium $= \pi (30)^2 \times 60 = 54\,000\pi$ cm$^3$.
Time $= \frac{54\,000\pi}{90\pi} = 600$ s $= 10$ minutes.
(b) Volume of water after 5 minutes $= 90\pi \times 300 = 27\,000\pi$ cm$^3$ (half the capacity, since 5 minutes is half of the time in (a)).
Volume of the sphere $= \frac{4}{3}\pi (15)^3 = 4500\pi$ cm$^3$.
If the water covers the sphere, the water and the sphere together fill the cylinder to depth $d$ cm:
$\pi (30)^2 d = 27\,000\pi + 4500\pi$
$900d = 31\,500$
$d = 35$
The top of the sphere is $2 \times 15 = 30$ cm above the base and $35 > 30$, so the sphere is covered and the depth is 35 cm.
(Tempting wrong answers: 30 cm, ignoring the sphere; 25 cm, subtracting the sphere's volume from the water.)
[(a) M1 for $90\pi$ cm$^3$ per second, or for the capacity divided by the flow with the units consistent; A1 for 10.
(b) M1 for $27\,000\pi$ (or half the capacity, taken from (a)); M1 for $(27\,000\pi + 4500\pi) \div 900\pi$; A1 for 35.
Accept 35 without a written check against 30 cm, but the check is kept in the published solution. The answers 30 (sphere ignored) and 25 (sphere subtracted) earn the first M1 only.]
question.syllabus_check: 4052 mensuration (volume of a cylinder and a sphere) with rate and speed (volume per second = cross-sectional area x speed; conversion of m/s to cm/s). The depth asked for is above the sphere, so no spherical cap is needed.
question.originality_note: Topic not asked this way before: no real paper 2002-2025 in the corpus and no earlier Set uses a pipe's flow rate or water displaced by a submerged solid. Set 1 P1 Q26 was a pyramid (height from an angle, volume, surface area); Set 1 P1 Q22 counted edges; Set 1 P2 Q9 was tank capacities and rainfall. GCE 2024 P1 Q26 and GCE 2025 P1 Q21 are partly-filled containers solved by similarity; this question uses no similarity. GCE 2006 P2 Q7 (hemisphere-cylinder tank draining at 3 litres per second) is a different container and gives the rate.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 10 minutes. The flow is pi(1.5)^2 x 40 = 90pi cm^3 per second and the capacity is pi(30)^2 x 60 = 54 000pi cm^3, so the aquarium fills in 600 s, which is 10 minutes.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 35 cm. After 5 minutes there is 27 000pi cm^3 of water, and the sphere's volume is (4/3)pi(15)^3 = 4500pi cm^3. The depth is 31 500pi / 900pi = 35 cm. Since 35 > 30, the top of the sphere, the sphere is covered and no spherical cap is needed. The sphere, 30 cm across, fits in the 60 cm cylinder. The wrong decisions give the tidy answers 30 (sphere ignored) and 25 (sphere subtracted).

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on 10 minutes and 35 cm, and my own working confirms both. The configuration is valid, since the water rises above the sphere.
fixes: Mark scheme: (a) M1 for 90pi cm^3 per second, or for the capacity divided by the flow with the units consistent; A1 for 10. (b) M1 for 27 000pi (or half the capacity, taken from (a)); M1 for (27 000pi + 4500pi) / 900pi; A1 for 35. Accept 35 without a written check against 30, but keep the check in the published solution. The answers 30 and 25 earn M1 only.

Light edit, optional: SEAB draws the container in every 2024/25 mensuration question (GCE 2024 P1 Q26, GCE 2025 P1 Q21). Add a sketch of the open cylindrical aquarium with the sphere resting on its base, not to scale. The words alone are enough.
verdict.why: Each part has its own decision. In (a) the candidate must supply the flow model, area x speed, with the m/s and diameter conversions hidden. In (b) the candidate must add the displaced volume rather than ignore or subtract it, then do a two-step routine. Both wrong routes land on believable whole numbers. This is the 2024/25 [2, 3] pattern of GCE 2025 P1 Q21 without its similarity, and it is as demanding and as clean as Set 1 P1 Q26. Set 1 P1 Q24 and P2 Q9 also put water in cylinders, but they test inverse proportion and capacity/rainfall, not a pipe's flow or a submerged solid, so the skills are new. Its rate skill also differs from those of Q18 and Q21 in this paper.
verdict.session_note: 23 Sep: polish: fix 1 (mark scheme). No sketch.

question.stem:
In the diagram, $ABCD$ is a trapezium in which $AD$ is parallel to $BC$ and $AD = 3BC$.
$\overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{p}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC} = \mathbf{q}$.
$E$ is the point on $CD$ such that $CE : ED = 1 : 2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
$F$ is the point on $AB$ such that $FE$ is parallel to $BC$.
Find the ratio $AF : FB$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The area of trapezium $ABCD$ is $45$ cm$^2$.
Find the area of quadrilateral $FBCE$.

skills: fix a point on a trapezium's slanting side by a parallel-vector condition, building the route through the longer parallel side and introducing the unknown ratio unprompted
vector along a side divided in a ratio measured from the far end ($\overrightarrow{DE} = \frac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{DC}$) with the longer parallel side as a multiple of the shorter
area of the part of a trapezium cut off by a line parallel to its parallel sides: the new parallel side from the vector result and the height scaled by the ratio
question.figure_description: A trapezium ABCD, with the label 'NOT TO SCALE' beside it. AD is the long lower side, horizontal; BC is the short upper side, horizontal and parallel to AD, about one third of the length of AD. A is at the bottom-left, D at the bottom-right, B at the top-left and C at the top-right; B lies above a point a little to the right of A and C lies above a point well to the left of D, so that AB and DC both slope inwards and ABCD is clearly a trapezium, not a parallelogram. The vertices are labelled A, B, C, D outside the figure. On side AB draw an arrowhead pointing from A towards B, labelled with the bold letter p beside the side. On side BC draw an arrowhead pointing from B towards C, labelled with the bold letter q above the side. Mark a point E on side CD, about one third of the way along CD from C towards D, with a small dot, labelled E outside the figure. Nothing else: do NOT draw or label the point F or the line FE, do not write any ratio, length, area, height or any other vector (in particular not 3q on AD), and do not shade any region.
question.solution:
(a) $AD$ is parallel to $BC$, in the same direction, and $AD = 3BC$, so $\overrightarrow{AD} = 3\mathbf{q}$.
$\overrightarrow{DC} = \overrightarrow{DA} + \overrightarrow{AB} + \overrightarrow{BC} = -3\mathbf{q} + \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{p} - 2\mathbf{q}$.
$CE : ED = 1 : 2$, so $DE = \frac{2}{3}DC$ and $\overrightarrow{DE} = \frac{2}{3}(\mathbf{p} - 2\mathbf{q}) = \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{p} - \frac{4}{3}\mathbf{q}$.
Let $\overrightarrow{AF} = k\mathbf{p}$.
$\overrightarrow{FE} = \overrightarrow{FA} + \overrightarrow{AD} + \overrightarrow{DE} = -k\mathbf{p} + 3\mathbf{q} + \frac{2}{3}\mathbf{p} - \frac{4}{3}\mathbf{q} = \left(\frac{2}{3} - k\right)\mathbf{p} + \frac{5}{3}\mathbf{q}$.
$FE$ is parallel to $BC$, so $\overrightarrow{FE}$ is a multiple of $\mathbf{q}$ and the coefficient of $\mathbf{p}$ is zero: $\frac{2}{3} - k = 0$, $k = \frac{2}{3}$.
$AF = \frac{2}{3}AB$ and $FB = \frac{1}{3}AB$, so $AF : FB = 2 : 1$.
(Route through $C$ instead: $\overrightarrow{FE} = \overrightarrow{FB} + \overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CE} = (1 - k)\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{q} + \frac{1}{3}(2\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p})$, the same vector.)
(Non-vector route by similar triangles: draw the line through $C$ parallel to $AB$, meeting $FE$ at $H$ and $AD$ at $G$. $ABCG$ and $FBCH$ are parallelograms, so $AG = BC$, $GD = 2BC$, $CG = AB$ and $CH = BF$. Triangles $CHE$ and $CGD$ are similar ($HE$ parallel to $GD$), so $\frac{CH}{CG} = \frac{CE}{CD} = \frac{1}{3}$, giving $BF = \frac{1}{3}AB$ and $AF : FB = 2 : 1$. Also $HE = \frac{1}{3}GD = \frac{2}{3}BC$, so $FE = BC + \frac{2}{3}BC = \frac{5}{3}BC$, as in (b).)
(Tempting wrong answer: $1 : 2$, copying the ratio $CE : ED$.)
(b) From (a), $\overrightarrow{FE} = \frac{5}{3}\mathbf{q}$, so $FE = \frac{5}{3}BC$.
Let $BC = b$ cm and let $h$ cm be the distance between $BC$ and $AD$. Since $FB = \frac{1}{3}AB$, the distance between $FE$ and $BC$ is $\frac{1}{3}h$.
Area of $ABCD = \frac{1}{2}(b + 3b)h = 2bh = 45$, so $bh = 22.5$.
$FBCE$ is a trapezium ($FE$ parallel to $BC$): area $= \frac{1}{2}\left(b + \frac{5}{3}b\right) \times \frac{1}{3}h = \frac{4}{9}bh = \frac{4}{9} \times 22.5 = 10$ cm$^2$.
(Tempting wrong answers: $15$, taking one third of the area because $FB = \frac{1}{3}AB$; $5$, scaling the area by $\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)^2$ as if the pieces were similar.)
Mark scheme.
(a) [4] M1 $\overrightarrow{DC} = \mathbf{p} - 2\mathbf{q}$ (or $\overrightarrow{CD} = 2\mathbf{q} - \mathbf{p}$) from $\overrightarrow{AD} = 3\mathbf{q}$; M1 $\overrightarrow{DE} = \frac{2}{3}\overrightarrow{DC}$ (or $\overrightarrow{CE} = \frac{1}{3}\overrightarrow{CD}$) in terms of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$; M1 $\overrightarrow{FE}$ in terms of an unknown multiple of $\mathbf{p}$ with the coefficient of $\mathbf{p}$ set to zero; A1 $2 : 1$. A non-vector route earns full marks only when it is justified by similar triangles (for example, by drawing the line through $C$ parallel to $AB$, or by producing $AB$ and $DC$ to meet), with the similar triangles named. A bare quotation of the result that a line parallel to the parallel sides of a trapezium divides the two slanting sides in the same ratio ($BF : FA = CE : ED = 1 : 2$), followed by $2 : 1$, earns at most B2.
(b) [2] B1 $FE = \frac{5}{3}BC$ (accept $FE = BC + \frac{1}{3}(AD - BC)$) together with the height $\frac{1}{3}h$ of $FBCE$, or area of $FBCE = \frac{4}{9}bh$; A1 $10$.
The answers $1 : 2$, $15$ and $5$ earn 0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 vectors in two dimensions: vector addition along a route, a point dividing a line in a given ratio, parallel vectors as scalar multiples with one unknown scalar; area of a trapezium. No three-dimensional vectors, no two-parameter intersection, no printed parameter.
question.originality_note: Set 1 P1 Q27 equated two vector routes to the intersection of the diagonals of a quadrilateral OABC (two parameters) and scaled a triangle's area to the whole quadrilateral by triangles sharing a height; this question uses a trapezium, fixes a point on a slanting side by a single parallel condition (one parameter, introduced by the candidate) and finds the area of a sub-trapezium from its new parallel side and a scaled height, not from triangles sharing a height. The [4, 2] weighting is the P1 closer's standard weight, not Set 1's content. GCE 2024 P1 Q27 (triangle OAB, show OC, two-parameter collinearity through a midpoint with m and n printed, triangle area) and GCE 2023 P1 Q27 (collinearity of O, P, Q) differ in configuration and in what is found; GCE 2019 P2 Q7(b)(iii) fixed a point by a trapezium condition in a triangle and asked only for a vector.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give AF : FB = 2 : 1. AD = 3q (AD is parallel to BC, same direction, three times as long), DC = p - 2q, DE = (2/3)(p - 2q). With AF = kp, FE = (2/3 - k)p + (5/3)q, and FE parallel to q forces k = 2/3. Checked with exact coordinates (A(0,0), B(1,3), C(4,3), D(9,0): E(17/3, 2), F(2/3, 2), AF/AB = 2/3). Proportional division gives the same result: BF : FA = CE : ED = 1 : 2. The trap 1 : 2 comes from reading the ratio the wrong way round.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 10 cm^2. FE = (5/3)BC and the height of FBCE is h/3, so the area is (1/2)(b + 5b/3)(h/3) = (4/9)bh. Since 2bh = 45, the area is 10. The coordinate check gives area FBCE / area ABCD = 4/18, and (4/18) x 45 = 10. The traps 15 (one third) and 5 (one ninth) are believable.

verdict.key_verdict: The setter and the blind examiner agree on both parts. My own vector working and an exact coordinate check confirm 2 : 1 and 10 cm^2.
fixes: Wording, to match SEAB's register: in (a), 'Find the ratio AF : FB.' (GCE 2024 P1 Q27(b): 'Find the ratio OQ : QB.')

Mark scheme, alternative route in (a): 4052 does not list the result 'a line parallel to the parallel sides of a trapezium divides the slanting sides in the same ratio'. So the non-vector route should earn full marks only when it is justified by similar triangles, for example by producing AB and DC to meet, or by drawing the line through C parallel to AB. A bare quotation of the result with 2 : 1 should earn at most B2. As written, a candidate who quotes the result earns 4 marks for one line.
Mark scheme, (b): split the M1 so that each idea earns credit. B1 for FE = (5/3)BC and the height h/3 of FBCE, or for area FBCE = (4/9)bh. A1 for 10.
verdict.why: Round 2 takes the round-1 fix: the ladder has gone and (a) is one unscaffolded [4]. The candidate turns AD = 3BC into AD = 3q, builds DE from the far end, and introduces the scalar for the parallel condition without a prompt. Then (b) [2] makes a new use of the vector result: the new parallel side is (5/3)BC and the height is scaled by 1/3. The numbers are clean and the traps land on 1 : 2, 15 and 5. The [4, 2] shape matches Set 1 P1 Q27 and the standard's own 6-7-mark shape (ii), but the skills are different: a one-parameter parallel condition in a trapezium, and a sub-trapezium area from its parallel sides and height, where Set 1 used a two-route diagonal intersection and triangles sharing a height. It is not a re-skin of GCE 2024 P1 Q27 (a triangle, a printed two-parameter collinearity, then a triangle area).
